On Sunday, March 1, 2015 at 3:38:15 PM UTC-5, Nathan L wrote:
> I would like to construct a binomial regression model in Stan using the Jeffery's prior (see http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2680313/) as part of my research efforts. I am not quite sure how to complete coding this model. Here is what I have so far.

For any manual adjustment to the value of the log-posterior distribution, you need to use the increment_log_prob() function, which is documented in chapter 16 of the user manual. In addition, I doubt you want to do all that calculation in the transformed parameters block because it will all get stored. You might declare log_lp at the top of the transformed parameters block and then do all that calculation inside a local block. That would store log_lp but not all the intermediate stuff. Or just do it all within the model block but that won't store the contribution of the Jeffrey's prior. Finally, you want to use increment_log_prob(0.5 * log_determinant(XTWX)) rather than increment_log_prob(0.5 * log(determinant(XTWX)))

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] parallel computing in Stan
messages.body_plain:
We haven't worked on parallelization of the log density
calculations.  The tricky part is dealing with autodiff.

I take it you mean the .hpp file that gets generated for a model?

>From what I gather from this:

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenMP

I think you'd actually need to add some explicit parallelism
constructs to the program.  We don't know how to do that with
autodiff.

If you have matrix operations and Eigen would use OpenMP somehow,
then there could be some gain.  See:

  http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicMultiThreading.html

But I'm not sure how to control it.  The autodiff code cannot be
run in parallel because we don't have any locking mechanism in
place, so there would be both race conditions leading to memory
conflicts and also ordering issues that wouldn't be resolved.

If you do manage to get some speedup, we'd love to hear about
it and would write it up in the next version of the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben!

WHOW!!! I tried it and it works like a charm... this is really a breakthrough for me.

Let me explain why: In my particular case I am dealing with PK (PD) problem which are notoriously complex models in the sense that it is very tedious to code them right. I assume the same arguments apply to any other more complex model. Now, the generated quantities block is a convenient place to do posterior checks, I agree. However, doing so glues together what does not necessarily has to go together which is inference and prediction. These are two different things and there are many reasons to do this in two steps:

- inference takes long, i.e. I worked with models which take 2-3 days per chain (noticing that I would need a different predictive check after two days hurts)
- to me there are two bits for prediction: first I want to predict my data I used to fit & (if I have) predict other external data to the model. Hence, this is anyway external to the model data set (and I often find more external data set when discussing with colleagues)
- then, after I have qualified my model, the fun part begins, which is "what-if", i.e. with PK problems I can start to ask - what if my next study is like XXX which forces me to simulate from the posterior
- even for fairly simple models this external prediction is very useful. Just imagine an unbalanced design for some covariates (let's say unbalanced due to problems here and there with sampling). By no means it is possible to foresee all those covariate combinations which may be of interest.

You are right that I need to watch out for random seeds, yes, but this I anyway have to do for any serious computation. In a nutshell, this makes the overall modelling process *much* more flexible as this allows me separate inference & prediction.

Some more comments:

- I would rename the function to something more general, to me this not just about testing a function, it is much more (flexible posterior simulation)
- You could go even further, i.e. you could create a function which takes as input everything from the data block and then provide the functions which correspond to the blocks, i.e.
* a transformed data block which would return a list of all transformed data variables (as a function of the input data)
* a transformed parameters function which takes as input the input data and all those parameters and returns the calculated transformed parameters
* a model function taking as input data & parameters (transformations can be automatically applied)

When is this functionality becoming part of the official rstan packages? Any time soon? I really hope so, just amazing!

Best,
Sebastian

They certainly could be used that way, but it seems a bit awkward to extract() the parameters and pass them to a function like this. > Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract Sampler Parameters in RStan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extract Sampler Parameters in RStan
messages.body_plain:
The magic key you're looking for is:

  get_adaptation_info

It IS in the doc.

> On Mar 2, 2015, at 11:58 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again, not having sampler parameters
> (accept stat, n divergent, etc) included in extract by default is dangerous.
> The user should be forced to look at these Clockwork Orange-style.

I agree that these should be included in extract, just like lp__.

> But I also can’t figure out how to access them from a stanfit object at
> all (there’s no official doc on how to do this and the archived users
> list is no help).  Seriously, why is this so hard?

In the doc for stanfit-class, you see:

  get_sampler_params
  signature(object = "stanfit"): obtain the parameters used for
  the sampler such as stepsizeand treedepth. The results are returned
  as a list, each element of which is an array for a chain. The array
  has number of columns corresponding to the number of parameters used
  in the sampler and its column names provide the parameter names. Optional
  parameter inc_warmup indicates whether to include the warmup period.

Here's an example:

  > fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(0,1); }")

  > samp_params <- get_sampler_params(fit);

At this point, samp_params[[1]] is the first chain, samp_params[[2]] is
the second chain and so on.  Each chain has everyting in order.

  > head(sps[[1]])
       accept_stat__ stepsize__ treedepth__ n_leapfrog__ n_divergent__
  [1,]  4.781267e-01  2.0000000           1            1             0
  [2,] 1.860020e-218  5.5698093           1            1             0
  [3,]  9.682160e-01  0.7105644           3            5             0
  [4,]  8.290335e-01  0.7877146           2            3             0
  [5,]  9.444573e-01  0.7123420           2            3             0
  [6,]  9.966285e-01  0.9768503           1            1             0

If you want to get rid of warmup, use

  get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)

but you probably don't for these since you've said we should be
paying attention to n_divergent__ in warmup.

It's in the R doc, but not under what you may be looking for,

This kind of doc issue (not knowing how the stanfit object was constructed
so not knowing what's in it by design) is one reason I don't like having single
classes or functions overloaded for different types of return types.
There's no way to provide clean doc for the get, because the columns
will vary based on the type of sampler (e.g., NUTS has treedepth__ but
vanilla HMC doesn't).  Similarly, stan() is used for the call for both vanilla
HMC and NUTS.  Just like in the command line.

- Bob

On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 9:39:09 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> How did you get  the doc for the stanfit class?  I tried
> all of the method()-like functions I could google but
> the best I could get was
>
> "> methods(class='stanfit')
> [1] as.array.stanfit*      as.data.frame.stanfit* as.matrix.stanfit*     dim.stanfit*
> [5] dimnames.stanfit*      is.array.stanfit*      pairs.stanfit*         print.stanfit*
>
>    Non-visible functions are asterisked"

Those aren't the methods you are looking for. More specifically, those are the S3 methods. You want the S4 methods, but you can't get them by doing

showMethods("stanfit-class")

because S4 methods are defined for generic functions with S4 classes as signatures instead of being part of the classes definition (like every other object-oriented language and the S4.5 classes in R, a.k.a. reference classes, which are not currently used by RStan but I am in favor of converting to). The shortest path to what you want probably would have been to look at all the functions exported by the rstan package and then guess what they do.

> ls("package:rstan")
 [1] "constrain_pars"      "extract"             "get_adaptation_info"
 [4] "get_cppcode"         "get_cppo_mode"       "get_cxxflags"
 [7] "get_inits"           "get_logposterior"    "get_num_upars"
[10] "get_posterior_mean"  "get_sampler_params"  "get_seed"
[13] "get_seeds"           "get_stancode"        "get_stanmodel"
[16] "grad_log_prob"       "log_prob"            "lookup"
[19] "makeconf_path"       "monitor"             "optimizing"
[22] "plot"                "read_rdump"          "read_stan_csv"
[25] "rstan_options"       "sampling"            "sflist2stanfit"
[28] "show"                "stan"                "stanc"
[31] "stan_model"          "stan_rdump"          "stan_version"
[34] "summary"             "testify"             "traceplot"
[37] "unconstrain_pars"

> And then was does get_sampler_params return?  It’s
> a list of what, exactly?  typeof() claims that it’s a double,
> but it’s single-indexed and it’s not at all clear how to
> extract a single sampler parameter.

It is a list whose length is equal to the number of chains. Each list element is an iterations x 4 matrix. It works almost like a std::vector except that you have to index it with double brackets. So,
my_list <- get_sampler_params(posterior)
my_list[[1]][2,3]
extracts the first list element and then the element in the second row and third column of that matrix. Typically, you would want to apply the same function to each chain, in which case it would be something like
sapply(my_list, FUN = colMeans)

Ben

On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 4:15:23 AM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> You are right that I need to watch out for random seeds, yes, but this I anyway have to do for any serious computation. In a nutshell, this makes the overall modelling process *much* more flexible as this allows me separate inference & prediction.

I improved the seed thing and it is pretty safe now. The only limitation is that the pseudo-random number generator is only initialized once at the first time a function that ends with _rng is called. You can pass a seed to it at this point but thereafter you cannot change the seed, unless you restart R.

> Some more comments:
>
> - I would rename the function to something more general, to me this not just about testing a function, it is much more (flexible posterior simulation)

I will think of a new name then

> - You could go even further, i.e. you could create a function which takes as input everything from the data block and then provide the functions which correspond to the blocks, i.e.
> * a transformed data block which would return a list of all transformed data variables (as a function of the input data)
> * a transformed parameters function which takes as input the input data and all those parameters and returns the calculated transformed parameters
> * a model function taking as input data & parameters (transformations can be automatically applied)

Users can (and probably should) write functions like this, but it would be hard to do so automatically by reparsing the C++ source.

> When is this functionality becoming part of the official rstan packages? Any time soon? I really hope so, just amazing!

It's in the GitHub version now (subject to renaming).

> On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 4:15:23 AM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > You are right that I need to watch out for random seeds, yes, but this I anyway have to do for any serious computation. In a nutshell, this makes the overall modelling process *much* more flexible as this allows me separate inference & prediction.
>
> I improved the seed thing and it is pretty safe now. The only limitation is that the pseudo-random number generator is only initialized once at the first time a function that ends with _rng is called. You can pass a seed to it at this point but thereafter you cannot change the seed, unless you restart R.
>
> > Some more comments:
> >
> > - I would rename the function to something more general, to me this not just about testing a function, it is much more (flexible posterior simulation)
>
> I will think of a new name then
>
> > - You could go even further, i.e. you could create a function which takes as input everything from the data block and then provide the functions which correspond to the blocks, i.e.
> > * a transformed data block which would return a list of all transformed data variables (as a function of the input data)
> > * a transformed parameters function which takes as input the input data and all those parameters and returns the calculated transformed parameters
> > * a model function taking as input data & parameters (transformations can be automatically applied)
>
> Users can (and probably should) write functions like this, but it would be hard to do so automatically by reparsing the C++ source.
>
> > When is this functionality becoming part of the official rstan packages? Any time soon? I really hope so, just amazing!
>
> It's in the GitHub version now (subject to renaming).
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] sampling from gamma
messages.body_plain:
The problem is this:

parameters {
  vector [N] u;
  ...
model {
  u ~ gamma (0.001, 0.001);
  ...

You need to constrain the variable u to be positive because
gamma() only has support on (0,inf).

And following Andrew, I'll beep at the extra spaces
before "[" and "(".  It makes the programs hard to read
because it violates standard formatting conventions.  To me,
i t  i s  l i k e   w r i t i n g  t e x t  l i k e  t h i s .

We seem to get a lot of creative spacing from users in Stan,
some of it derived from R's unusual conventions, such as

  return(x)  vs.   return x

  if(foo)     vs.   if (foo)

  line breaks to denote ends of statements    vs.  semicolons

I find the ones on the left hard to read --- every other language
I know conventionally uses the forms on the right (other than
Python, which uses spaces and line breaks;  Lisp and its descendants
where it's all parens, and make, which uses tabs).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 6:16:27 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 10:39:25 PM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> >
> > It would still entail two compilations because the C++ source used to expose the user-defined functions is a shortened and heavily modified version of the C++ source used to draw from the posterior.
>
> Why does it need to be modified?  And how are you modifying it?

It ignores everything starting with the class definition for the model (because that isn't relevant to the user-defined functions)
It takes away the local namespace (because Rcpp can only expose functions from the global namespace), which entails cutting all the using:: statements from what used to be the local namespace and pasting them inside the user-defined functions (so as not to create conflicts in the global namespace)
It gets rid of all the templating (because R can only use double or int)
All the user-defined functions that end in _rng have their arguments rewired to not pass a RNG& (because Rcpp can't deal with it). Instead they get an int& seed = 0 argument and at the first line of the body of the function is inserted as static boost::ecuyer1988 base_rng__(seed);. Thus, that gets initialized once with the initial seed but has global scope.
All the user-defined functions that end in _rng have their arguments rewired to not pass a T_lp_accum__& (because we can't template). Instead that is deleted and the first line of the body of the function is inserted as stan::math::accumulator<double> lp_accum__;.
All the user-defined functions have their arguments rewired to not pass a std::ostream* pstream__ (because Rcpp can't deal with it). Instead that is deleted and the first or second line of the body of the function is inserted as std::ostream* pstream__ = &Rcpp::Rcout;. Thus, if the user-defined function has print() statements, the Rcpp::Rcout thing makes sure they end up in R somehow.
All the inline declarations get taken away for some reason I can't remember (probably a Rcpp limitation)
The relevant functions (but not their declarations if there are declarations) get marked with the attribute // [[Rcpp::export]] before their definitions
A variety of things get deleted from the corresponding functors. Perhaps the functors themselves should be deleted because I don't think they can be called from R anyway.
Everything that looks like a templated type gets changed to a double, inclusive of all the internal const static bool propto__ = true; being changed to false so that (correct) log-density calculations will match those in R (if Stan is using the same parameterization)
There is some special handling of get_lp()
Dependencies are added to StanHeaders, BH, RcppEigen, and Rcpp so that it can find its #includes (because the compiler is not provided our ordinary CFLAGS)

That's all. So, yes it probably will be a nightmere to maintain, but all of that was a result of it first failing to compile without it. So, if that is the price that we have to pay for users to be able to test their user-defined functions (and Sebastian can do his posterior predictive stuff outside of generated quantities) then so be it. It would be good to have a test .stan file with every conceivable kind of valid user-defined function (Sebastian got 90% of the way there by himself), so that Travis or something could alert us when it inevitably gets broken. Ideally, as far as making something like this a feature that the other Stan interfaces could support, it would probably be better to have a flag that could be passed to stanc so that it would emit C++ code that would obviate the need for as many of the above tweaks as possible. But that would require a significant undertaking on the part of someone who understands stanc whereas my approach just requires a significant undertaking on the part of someone who understands regexes.

messages.subject: Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
messages.subject_clean: Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to ask for some model guidance. I apologise in advance if my problem seems trivial, but my experience with Bayesian models is limited.

I am trying to identify mixtures in a population, in which each data point has its own profile. The tricky part is that each data point may be a member of multiple mixtures. From what I have found so far, this can be modelled using the so-called "Indian Buffet Process" (IBP) (Griffiths et al., 2011). However, as I have been able to read in the reference and on the board, Stan does not (yet) handle these kind of infinite models. From other threads on this forum, I have seen people have been mimicking the Chinese Restaurant Process using a very large number of mixtures. Can, or have, something similar been done for the IBP?

I am not even sure this is the best model to use, but I do not know of any better. To go a bit more into detail, the data is a NxM matrix, in which there are N data points and M measurements. The measurements are continous and (approximately) normally distributed (on log scale). Each data point has a lot of measurements with a zero value, simply because nothing was detected.

I have tried to come up with a complete description, but if anything is missing, please do ask!

Thanks in advance.

Cheers,
David

messages.body_plain:
Trivial's a matter of perspective --- almost everything's
hard the first time and trivial after the tenth time.

It doesn't sound like you have an infinite mixture if you have
a fixed number of columns.  From Griffith's and Gharamani's
abstract ( https://cocosci.berkeley.edu/tom/papers/indianbuffet.pdf ):

  The Indian buffet process is a stochastic process defining
  a probability distribution over equiva- lence classes of sparse
  binary matrices with a finite number of rows and an unbounded number
  of columns. This distribution is suitable for use as a prior
  in probabilistic models that represent objects using a potentially
  infinite array of features, or that involve bipartite graphs in
  which the size of at least one class of nodes is unknown.

The thing to do when building a Bayesian model is to consider how
the data is generated (here it sounds like some kind of measurement
process).  Could you say a bit more about what the
colummns are and how the zero entries come about if the measurements
are approximately lognormal (0 isn't going to come out of a lognormal
observation)?  For example, is it a censoring process that truncates
low measurements to zero?  If so, you probably just want a model to
account for the censoring.    Is there any relation among the columns
or are they all different kinds of measurements?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It could be me that read it wrong. I was thinking of it as mixture model with an infinite number of mixtures, in which each data point could be member of multiple mixtures.

Yes, it is indeed a measurement process. Each "feature" is the same measurement, measured under slightly different conditions. What we expect is that feature 1 is correlated to feature 2, and feature 2 to 3, ..., approximately until we measure 0 (absence). The standard in my field is to work with log-values, so I use the log(value+1) transformation to avoid the log(0) errors, and this is (approximately) normally distributed, excluding the 0 measurements.

To give an example:

A = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 2.3, 4.5]
B = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
C = [0, 0, , 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2.9, 2.2, 4.4]

So A would have the profile [4.5, 5, 6] and [3, 2.3, 4.5]. What I would like to identify is that point A has two mixtures (1 and 2), B has one mixture (1) and C has one mixture (2). Thus mixture 1 consists of A+B, and mixture 2 consists of A+C.

I hope the explanation was clear.

Cheers,
David

It's for infinitely fat mixtures.  If you have finitely
many columns and model each one, then there's only finitely
many.  It's the "unbounded number of columns" part that
your data's missing.

> Yes, it is indeed a measurement process. Each "feature" is the same measurement, measured under slightly different conditions. What we expect is that feature 1 is correlated to feature 2, and feature 2 to 3, ..., approximately until we measure 0 (absence).

It would probably help if you could be more specific (less abstract)
about what these measurements are.

A mixture would indeed give you that correlation.

> The standard in my field is to work with log-values, so I use the log(value+1) transformation to avoid the log(0) errors, and this is (approximately) normally distributed, excluding the 0 measurements.

> B = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
> C = [0, 0, , 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2.9, 2.2, 4.4]
>
> So A would have the profile [4.5, 5, 6] and [3, 2.3, 4.5].

Is that the result of log(measurement + 1) or the raw measurements
that you'll add 1 to and take the log?

Is there some physical correspondence to a profile here?

> What I would like to identify is that point A has two mixtures (1 and 2), B has one mixture (1) and C has one mixture (2). Thus mixture 1 consists of A+B, and mixture 2 consists of A+C.

Does the order of the columns matter?  For instance, are
they measurements over time?   Clearly the behavior isn't
continuous, because you go from 8 down to 0 in one step.  But
the values close to each other look related in A.  That would
matter in terms of how you'd want to model it.

Then the question is what do you expect the relationship to
be between A's and B's measurement.  It looks like B has
one of the components of A and C has one of the components
of A.

If so, you might want something like a change point
time-series model.  The data for A is probably three mixtures,
if you include the zeroes.  You want to model the entire
data generating process, including generating the zeroes.

So a simple model might assume some number of mixture components K,
each with means mu[k] and std devs sigma[k], and then each
row would start in one of the comonents, continue to draw from
that mixture for some number of observations, then drop to 0 or
another mixture.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
OK, I think I see this a bit better.  What you probably want
to be looking at in the way of non-parametrics is a Dirichlet
process prior on the number of mixture components.  That would
let the K in my earlier comment be given a prior.  If you
have a reasonable upper bound, this can be well approximated with
a finite upper bound on K.

And no, you wouldn't associate each row with a single mixture
component.  You'd have something like this for row n:

  x[n,1], x[n,2], ..., x[n,M]

and maybe some kind of process for generating a sequence of
components where lambda[n,m] in 1:K is the mixture from which
x[n,m] is drawn,

  lambda[n,1], ..., lambda[n,M]

Then you'd want to put a model on how the lambda values transition.
An HMM would be a general way to do it, but they're not very good
at modeling length --- you only get exponential decay beyond a certain
finite memory limit.  That's what I was calling the change-point structure.

Thanks for the extra detail on the process --- I'll have to

about the unbounded mixture components.  As Bob alluded
to in his first email, the only way this will work in Stan is if
you threshold the number of mixture components a priori
and hope that your posterior mass concentrates away from
that threshold.

messages.body_plain:
Here's a function that will return the max treedepth for each chain. If you change "treedepth__" to any of the other sampler params and change "max" whatever function you want then you can pretty much get any sampler param info you want using this template.

max_treedepth <- function(stanfit, inc_warmup = TRUE) {
  max_td <- sapply(get_sampler_params(stanfit, inc_warmup = inc_warmup),
                   function(x) max(x[,"treedepth__"]))
  names(max_td) <- paste0("chain", 1:length(max_td))
  max_td
}

If you don't feel like writing each of those functions, I've already done most of them for you and whole bunch of others. There's a handy little convenience function in the shinyStan package called stan_get that you can call from R.  See help("stan_get", "shinyStan").

y = f(x; \theta) + w

where y are the measurents, x are (deterministic) control variables and \theta are the model parameters to be estimated. f() is a nonlinear deterministic function and w are measurement errors drawn from a known distribution. The parameters of this distribution are generally known, however it would useful to infer them as well of course. What would be interesting is to explore the shape of the posterior p( \theta | y,x ) for different "measurement configurations".

-Arrigo

messages.body_plain:
You want better priors for a start.  We have a few sections in
the regression chapter of the book, which summarize some of
Andrew's papers on the topic which provide more info on why
things like gamma(0.001,0.001) are so bad.

You may also need to reparameterize some of this in order
to get efficiency.

I don't see anything intrinsically wrong with the model, but
it's rather dense reading.

One thing to do (after trimming the 200K iterations down to
something reasonable) is to do a pairs plot to see if there
are lots of correlations among variables, as they can indicate
non-identifiability.  The other thing I'd recommend is
lowering the initial step size and the target acceptance
rate --- both of these can make the sampler more stable.
Are you getting warning messages now?

The other thing to do is insert print statements to see if
some of the calculations are underflowing or overflowing
or otherwise arithmetically unstable --- this can happen in larger
data sets even if smaller ones are OK.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] WBIC in rstan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] WBIC in rstan
messages.body_plain:
These are fundamentally different models.

Your programs have the same data, transformed data, and
paramters:

data {
  int N;
  vector[N] x;
  vector[N] y;
}
transformed data {
  matrix[N,2] X;
  real Nr;

  Nr <- N;
  for (n in 1:N) {
      X[n,1] <- 1.0;
      X[n,2] <- x[n];
  }
}
parameters {
  vector[2] beta;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

The difference is in the log density function:

wbic_test.stan
------------------------------
model {
  increment_log_prob(1/log(Nr) * normal_log(y, X * beta, sigma));
}

wbic_test_2.stan
-----------------------
model {
  y ~ normal(X * beta, sigma);
}

If you look at the log densities (up to an additive constant)
in the two programs, you have:

test.stan:

  1/log(Nr) * (-log(sigma) - 0.5 * ((y - X * beta) / sigma)^2

test_2.stan:

  -log(sigma) - 0.5 * ((y - X * beta) / sigma)^2

Because the posterior density is proportional to these, it
varies between the two models.

- Bob

> On Mar 4, 2015, at 7:10 PM, Ishikura Kiwamu <ishikur...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Soga
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract Sampler Parameters in RStan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extract Sampler Parameters in RStan
messages.body_plain:
You really want to look at the entire distribution of each diagnostic
variable aggregated across the chains, so in the end I had to do

sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'treedepth__']))[,1]

In PyStan it’s a similar problem but reduce makes it slightly cleaner,

sampler_params = fit.get_sampler_params(inc_warmup=False)
reduce(lambda x, y: x + y['n_divergent__'].tolist(), sampler_params, [])

messages.subject: Re: Weibull regression failed to converge in Rstan
messages.subject_clean: Weibull regression failed to converge in Rstan
messages.body_plain:
I've had a similar experience with a different Weibull model, but I think the problem is more general than the Weibull model.  In my case subsetting the data worked well but with the full data most chains would give a much broader posterior (restricted mostly by the prior) .  Sometimes one out of ten chains would find the true posterior which was very narrow.  My understanding is that in the failed cases Stan adapted to exploring the much broader space and managed to skip over the true, very sharp, peak in the posterior.  Decreasing the initial step size helped but without good starting values it was still unreliable.  Optimization (I recall) had a similar problem though it was more likely to complain of numerical issues.

I resolved it by running a series of models with increasing amounts of data.  For more complex models this required doing stratified subsets of the data to make sure each group had enough data to be estimated.  I ended up using something like a series of three or four models, each with an increasing amount of data, and always took the inital values from samples of a previous model.  I think the same could be achieved by raising the posterior to a power during adaptation but adaptation is hairy enough as it is so I never got around to messing with it.

On a side-note, this issue goes away if your model is complex enough in the right way---that is you spread out that data over enough parameters.

Hope that helps,

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
messages.body_plain:
> On 03 Mar 2015, at 16:55, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The IBP is just a certain implementation of a Dirichlet process
> prior.  Because we don’t handle discrete parameters you’d have
> to think about the collapsed IBP, but then you still have to worry
> about the unbounded mixture components.  As Bob alluded
> to in his first email, the only way this will work in Stan is if
> you threshold the number of mixture components a priori
> and hope that your posterior mass concentrates away from
> that threshold.

Yes, that is also what I deduced from previous threads on the board. Is there a process that would shrink the number of mixtures the model use, so to speak? Or how would I go about checking the posterior mass concentrates away?

>
> On Mar 3, 2015, at 3:35 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > OK, I think I see this a bit better.  What you probably want
> > to be looking at in the way of non-parametrics is a Dirichlet
> > process prior on the number of mixture components.  That would
> > let the K in my earlier comment be given a prior.  If you
> > have a reasonable upper bound, this can be well approximated with
> > a finite upper bound on K.
> >
> > And no, you wouldn't associate each row with a single mixture
> > component.  You'd have something like this for row n:
> >
> > x[n,1], x[n,2], ..., x[n,M]
> >
> > and maybe some kind of process for generating a sequence of
> > components where lambda[n,m] in 1:K is the mixture from which
> > x[n,m] is drawn,
> >
> > lambda[n,1], ..., lambda[n,M]
> >
> > Then you'd want to put a model on how the lambda values transition.

That is actually a very good and interesting idea. Can you recommend any literature on this (apart from the Stan reference)?

> > An HMM would be a general way to do it, but they're not very good
> > at modeling length --- you only get exponential decay beyond a certain
> > finite memory limit.  That's what I was calling the change-point structure.

Not sure I follow here. My knowledge of HMMs are limited to the very basics.

Cheers,
David

> >
> > Thanks for the extra detail on the process --- I'll have to
> > think a bit more about that.  The point's just that you want
> > to model that process as closely as you can in the statistical
> > model.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Mar 4, 2015, at 2:22 AM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > > On 03 Mar 2015, at 14:28, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > On Mar 4, 2015, at 12:01 AM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > It could be me that read it wrong. I was thinking of it as mixture model with an infinite number of mixtures, in which each data point could be member of multiple mixtures.
> > > >
> > > > It's for infinitely fat mixtures.  If you have finitely
> > > > many columns and model each one, then there's only finitely
> > > > many.  It's the "unbounded number of columns" part that
> > > > your data's missing.
> > > >
> > >
> > > I see. I might have to re-read the paper. It seems I misunderstood the concept.
> > >
> > > >
> > > > > Yes, it is indeed a measurement process. Each "feature" is the same measurement, measured under slightly different conditions. What we expect is that feature 1 is correlated to feature 2, and feature 2 to 3, ..., approximately until we measure 0 (absence).
> > > >
> > > > It would probably help if you could be more specific (less abstract)
> > > > about what these measurements are.
> > > >
> > >
> > > Ok, I will try to exemplify the process in more detail, still keeping it a bit abstract.
> > >
> > > Imagine a lane. On the lane, there are different obstacles, varying in size (getting larger as one moves down the lane). Now along comes two components A and B, which are physically connected. They move down the lane until they cannot proceed any further due to obstacles. Next comes A and C, which are also physically connected. C is, however, slightly smaller than B, and the A-C component can move further down the lane. The number A-B and A-C are typically in the millions, and what we count is not the actual number of A-B components, but A and B individually (typically these are in millions++, so we use the log(count+1) transformation). Not all of the components stops the exact same place (hence they have a profile).
> > >
> > > I hope that made it a bit more clear!
> > >
> > > > A mixture would indeed give you that correlation.
> > > >
> > > > > The standard in my field is to work with log-values, so I use the log(value+1) transformation to avoid the log(0) errors, and this is (approximately) normally distributed, excluding the 0 measurements.
> > > > >
> > > > > To give an example:
> > > > >
> > > > > A = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 2.3, 4.5]
> > > > > B = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
> > > > > C = [0, 0, , 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2.9, 2.2, 4.4]
> > > > >
> > > > > So A would have the profile [4.5, 5, 6] and [3, 2.3, 4.5].
> > > >
> > > > Is that the result of log(measurement + 1) or the raw measurements
> > > > that you'll add 1 to and take the log?
> > > > Is there some physical correspondence to a profile here?
> > > >
> > >
> > > Depends what you mean by physical. Each entry is an actual count of the component. I.e. A[0], B[0], and C[0] (using array index notation) are from the exam same place on the lane.
> > >
> > > > > What I would like to identify is that point A has two mixtures (1 and 2), B has one mixture (1) and C has one mixture (2). Thus mixture 1 consists of A+B, and mixture 2 consists of A+C.
> > > >
> > > > Does the order of the columns matter?  For instance, are
> > > > they measurements over time?   Clearly the behavior isn't
> > > > continuous, because you go from 8 down to 0 in one step.  But
> > > > the values close to each other look related in A.  That would
> > > > matter in terms of how you'd want to model it.
> > > >
> > >
> > > Yes, these values should indeed be related.
> > >
> > > > Then the question is what do you expect the relationship to
> > > > be between A's and B's measurement.  It looks like B has
> > > > one of the components of A and C has one of the components
> > > > of A.
> > >
> > > Yes, that was exactly the point I was trying to make with the example. And this is why I was looking into infinite mixture models. Essentially we don’t know how many mixtures there are, or how many mixtures each component can be part of. We want to be informed by the data about this (with some prior assumptions).

messages.subject: Diagnosing HMC/NUTS sampler, sampler parameters, manuals, shinyStan, (feature suggestions)
messages.subject_clean: Diagnosing HMC/NUTS sampler, sampler parameters, manuals, shinyStan, (feature suggestions)
messages.body_plain:
Dear stan users and developers,

I am currently trying to improve model estimation by modifying some sampler parameters. Here are a few suggestions about how this could be made easier from the perspective of a user.
(Note that I am using “sampler parameter” both for the user-settable parameters like max_treedepth and for the parameters reported like treedepth)

In short:

1)      Consolidate and improve description of key sampler parameters that should be investigated or could be changed by the user
2)      Be clearer about which aspect (pre/post warmup, distribution, mean, max?) of the reported sampler parameters is most relevant
3)      Show sampler parameters  when using print(stanfit) in rstan
4)      Where to find sampler parameter in a stanfit object
5)      Show distributions of sampler parameters and parameter settings in shiny stan

In detail:

1) Sampler parameter description

>From browsing through and reading in the the cmdstan guide, the stan reference, and the rstan manual I got the impression that the sampler parameters a less unexperienced user (like me) might want to play with are the target acceptance rate, jittering of step size, and maximum treedepth.

I found the description of these parameters in the cmdstan manual the clearest. The stan reference does not seem to detail default parameters values, and rstan manual does not do a lot of explaining. I think the reader could benefit if there would be only one description (I’d prefer in the stan reference), to which the other manuals point at a prominent place.

One thing I think would also help is to have a brief discussion of these key parameters together, in addition to their description in section for HMC and nuts parameters respectively. This joint discussion could also suggest which parameters one could try to change first (if this can be said) and describe how they interact in their effect on acceptance rate, estimation time etc.

2) Which aspects of the sampler parameters should one check?

>From Michael B.’s recent post on the list I infer that one should examine the entire distribution of the treedepth parameter. I am not sure if this is also said so in the manuals. Maybe one could add/highlight this point? In this context it would also be good to know what constitutes a “bad” distribution. Is it ok when 0, 1, 5, 10 or how many percent of the samples reach the maximum tree depth? Should I be more interested in the warmup or the sampling period.

3) Sampler parameter statistics in print(stanfit)

That works nicely in cmdstan and it would be nice to also have it in rstan (I haven’t use pystan).

4) Which sampler parameters were used?

Maybe I am only overlooking this, but I couldn’t find where in the stanfit object the sampler parameters used are stored (e.g.  max_treedepth, adapt_delta, …).

5) Sampler parameters in shinyStan

The diagnosis tab of shinyStan is very useful. I think it would be even more useful if the sub-tab HMC/NUTS would also show which sampler parameters were used for the current model, and if, following Michael B.’s point, it would show distributions in addition to or instead of the stats. A reference to the section of the stan reference in which the sampler parameters are explained in more detail would also be helpful (or just copy paste the entire section, which would be the most user friendly).

Related, it would be nice if the tab that shows trace plot also had a pop-up window in which feature of “bad” chains are described.

I realize that these are things the user should know, but if shinyStan is thought as a way to make stan as accessible as possible to new users, collecting all information needed to evaluate the model in one place is a useful.

Cheers - Guido

messages.body_plain:
For the R functions, maybe a wrapper for print would be cool where the user could supply with_pars or without_pars (not both I guess, as that would be confusing) instead of just pars to make it easier to exclude a few parameters. A quick, crude, way of doing it would be

stan_print <- function(x, with_pars, without_pars, ...) {
  wp <- !missing(with_pars)
  wop <- !missing(without_pars)

  if (wp & wop) stop("Specify only one of 'with_pars' and 'without_pars'")
  if (!(wp | wop)) return(print(x, ...))
  if (wp) return(print(x, pars = with_pars, ...))
  else print(x, pars = x@sim$pars_oi[!x@sim$pars_oi %in% without_pars], ...)
}

So then stan_print(stanfit) does the default print(stanfit), stan_print(stanfit, with_pars = c("a", "b")) does print(stanfit, pars = c("a", "b")) and stan_print(stanfit, without_pars = c("a","b")) does what Juan suggested for removing parameters from the output.

messages.subject: How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.subject_clean: How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.body_plain:
I have a Markov chain model with four states A, B, C and D. The transition probabilities are given by the 4x4 transition matrix M. The data are given as chains of states e.g. AAABBBACCCAA .... How would you parametrize this model?  How would you parametrize a hierarchical extension of the model? For hierarchical extension assume that I have N subjects and for each subject I have M_n chains.

Idea 1: Estimate transition probabilities directly. I would then use inverse logit to transform the transition probabilities and pool the transformed vars with a hierarchical gaussian prior.

Idea 2: In the actual data, the states repeat very often. Same-state chains of length 100 and more are not unusual. As a consequence the values on the diagonal of the transition matrix will be near 1 and other elements will be near 0. My alternative idea is to estimate the transition probabilities between different consecutive states. I would estimate the length of a chain of same-state transitions with a poisson model. Again, there is a multilevel generalization of poisson model in chap. 15 of gelman's DAUR&MHM. I would adapt this.

I haven't coded anything yet. I'm just interested in your opinion. Which idea is better or do you see alternative formulations?

My hunch is that idea 2 is easier to estimate with STAN and also the parameters are easier to interpret. However, I've never seen idea 2 in the literature, so I'm not very confident.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.body_plain:
Hi -

Idea 2 is called the "semi-Markov model". I hope that helps your
literature search :)
Egotistically enough, I'll point you to a short note I wrote recently
about what to call them:
http://rspb.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/281/1792/20141370.e-letters

In response to the question about choosing between the MM and SMM, I'd
say choose whichever fits closest to your beliefs about the underlying
behaviour. Note that a non-hidden Markov model will always generate
"holding times" of geometrically-distributed length. If a priori you
don't think that fits well to your situation, then that's a good
argument to use your SMM.

Best
Dan

> > >
> > >
> > > stan_print <- function(x, with_pars, without_pars, ...) {

> > >   wop <- !missing(without_pars)

> > > So then stan_print(stanfit) does the default print(stanfit), stan_print(stanfit, with_pars = c("a", "b")) does print(stanfit, pars = c("a", "b")) and stan_print(stanfit, without_pars = c("a","b")) does what Juan suggested for removing parameters from the output.

messages.body_plain:
That shouldn't be hard. You just have to create another local block within the transformed parameters block.

transformed parameters {
  real keep;
  {
    vector exclude;
    ...
    keep <- f(exclude);
  }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.body_plain:
If you define transition matrix M per individual (M_i) and use M_i for all chains of states for a given individual, you can use a dirichlet hyperprior for columns of transition probabilities in your transition matrix M_i. However, this would only pool information for each column separately, and not account for possible correlation between column within a given matrix M_i. I don't know whether there are priors for whole transition matrices - perhaps this is something you can find literature.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.body_plain:
The simplest thing to do would be what Luc suggested --- use a Dirichlet
prior and give it some kind of hyperprior (typically reparameterizing
in terms of a simplex mean alpha/sum(alpha) and a prior on the total
count sum(alpha).  Then each state would draw its transition probabilities
from Dirichlet(alpha).

You could enrich this using a logistic multinormal.  Just use
a multivariate normal, then softmax transform the draws to get
your simplexes for the transitions.  This was one of the first
pieces of stats advice Andrew ever gave me, long before we
started working together.

- Bob

matters.  That's the only difference in the two programs (other

to do with the refactoring of error handling types that was

labeled it as such.

messages.subject_clean: optimizing the ODE integrator
messages.body_plain:

The ODE integrator currently has to deal with the ODE itself and it's sensitivities. Now, the sensitivities depend on the particular parametrization of the ODE, right? messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How would you parametrize a markov chain model and its hierarchical extension?
messages.body_plain:
As I'm riding my bike home, I realise my previous post was (partly) hogwash.

For identifiability, only fix the sd of the multinormal hyperprior for alpha_u; the mean vector is a parameter to be estimated. Further, for identifiability, you may fix the first element of each of the N sets of length N to the value 1.

Unfortunately, I don't see a way to implement the mu + u*L trick here to simulate the multinormal random alpha_raw, as the results of this trick needs to be positive (for the softmax). Will a call to multinormal_cholesky be very ineffecient?

The correct pseudo code then becomes (somebody please correct me if I'm wrong):

parameters:
corr_cholesky[N] L;
vector<lower=0>[N] alpha_sum;  // column-specific sample sizes for Dirichlet prior for transition probabilities

vector<lower=0>[N*N] alpha_u_mu;   // mean untransformed alpha (each column of the transition matrix has it's own N-vector)
vector<lower=0>[N*N)] alpha_raw;  // untransformed alpha

model block:
vector[N*(N-1)] alpha_raw;

matrix[N,N] alpha; // each column is a vector of alpha parameters of the dirichlet prior for a column

alpha_u ~ normal(0, 1);
L ~ lkj_prior(...);  // if you want something else than a uniform prior

alpha_raw ~ multinormal_cholesky(alpha_u_mu, L);  // I don't see a way to comobine the support of alpha_raw
                                                  // with the mu + u*L trick.

for (n in 1:N) {  // not sure the indexing is right here, check that values are organized into columns
  alpha[n] <- to.column(softmax(n-th set of N elements from alpha_raw) .* alpha_sum[n]);
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] optimizing the ODE integrator
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] optimizing the ODE integrator
messages.body_plain:
> The ODE integrator currently has to deal with the ODE itself and it's sensitivities. Now, the sensitivities depend on the particular parametrization of the ODE, right? If so, then the way the user chooses the parametrization has a big impact on the performance of Stan, i.e. if a bad parametrization leads to stiff sensititivies, then this a bad thing!

Yup, this is fundamental to how ODEs are defined (at least unless you define them
purely geometrically).

> Am I right here and if yes, then what techniques can you recommend to optimize?

There is no general procedure here.  Of course it would be great if our ODEs
were all linear, but they don’t be in any practical model and the best we can hope
for is that they are not _too_ nonlinear where we evaluate them.  In Bayesian
inference this is even more complicated because we don’t get to choose where
we evaluate the ODEs, the data and model assumptions define that.

In particular, we haven’t been running ODE models in Stan long enough to even
identify that many pathological models, let alone classify them by the interaction
between the parameterization and the nonlinearity of the ODEs in an attempt
to identify efficient parameterization strategies.

messages.subject: matrix column indexing bounds check bug in Stan 2.6
messages.subject_clean: matrix column indexing bounds check bug in Stan 2.6
messages.body_plain:
There's a pretty serious bug in our bounds checking for
matrices that was introduced in Stan 2.6.

If you have a matrix with more cols than rows, and try
to index past the number of columns, Stan will throw an error.
For example, this will throw an error but shouldn't:

  matrix[2,3] z;
  for (m in 1:2)
    for (n in 1:3)
      y <- y + z[m,n];

It will throw as soon as n > 2.

If you don't have matrices with more columns than rows that
you are indexing directly, you won't tickle this bug with 2.6.

We have it fixed on a branch (currently undergoing full
integration testing) and will be doing a 2.6.1 release ASAP.

The good news is we're also removing the long long type (we
figured out how to ifdef it so it would still work with 64-bit
Windows's crazy decision to make long types 32 bits).  This was
the last obstacle to getting RStan onto CRAN, so expect to
see RStan on CRAN soon after the 2.6.1 release.

Sorry for any inconvenience this might cause.

- Bob

P.S.  Many thanks to Aki Vehtari for finding the bug and providing
      a simple A-B test case that let us diagnose the problem
      quickly.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the  nice drawing --- that's the banana posterior
(Rosenbrock created a famous test case based on it that
Michael sometimes uses for illustration.)

Yes, a dense mass matrix is worse because the curvature
varies.  The thing to do for NUTS is set a higher acceptance
rate target (adapt_delta) and a lower initial step size (stepsize).
That will force the Hamiltonian simulation to take smaller
steps and follow the curvature better.  This is roughly the
suggestion that Luke Bornn et al. make in the comment on
Girolami and Calderhead's paper --- there's a critical step size
above which you'll have very bad approximations to the Hamiltonian.
Euclidean HMC and Euclidean NUTS just uses a first-order approximation
based on the gradient.

Yes, NUTS should do better than vanilla HMC.

Yes, RHMC (with geoNUTS, of course) should be even better.
Michael Betancourt has some wonderful animations relating to this.

We're hoping to get RHMC out some time soon (maybe in a few
months).  All it's waiting on is us to sort out some of the
final issues with higher-order autodiff --- RHMC is already
implemented on a branch, it just won't work for general models
yet until the higher-order autodiff catches up.

- Bob

Were the other observations and censored and if so, do you know
how many censorings were done for the data set?

Otherwise, if you just simulate from a model and throw
some of the observations away, you shouldn't expect to
recover the parameters because the model doesn't match the
data generation process.

For example, consider generating data according to normal(0,1)
and then throwing away any negative observations.  You're not
going to expect a sample mean of 0 or sample sd of 1.

To do this right, you need to record how many observations were
below 0 and use the normal cdf to model them.

There's a chapter in the manual on data censoring.

- Bob

much like a banana) are indicative of multiplicative non-identifiabilities in
your likelihood, i.e. something like

y ~ normal(a * b, sigma);

later.  If you can’t figure out from where in your model the non-identifiability
is coming then you have to wait for Riemannian, which means waiting for
the autodiff.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
messages.body_plain:
I recommend as an easy default option
 nu ~ gamma(2,0.1);

This was proposed and anlysed by Juárez and Steel (2010) (Model-based clustering of non-Gaussian panel data based on skew-t distributions. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 28, 52–66.). Juárez and Steel compere this to Jeffreys prior and report that the difference is small.  Simpson et al (2014) (arXiv:1403.4630) propose a theoretically well justified "penalised complexity (PC) prior", which they show to have a good behavior for the degrees of freedom, too. PC prior might be the best choice, but requires numerical computation of the prior (which could computed in a grid and interpolated etc.). It would be feasible to implement it in Stan, but it would require some work. Unfortunately no-one has compared PC prior and this gamma prior directly, but based on the discussion with Daniel Simpson, although PC prior would be better this gamma(2,0.1) prior is not a bad choice. Thus, I would use it until someone implements the PC prior for degrees of freedom of the Student's t in Stan.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 6, 2015, at 7:06 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for clarifying! Regarding the following piece:
>
> vector[M] theta_raw[M];
> for (m in 1:M)
>   theta_raw[m] ~ multi_normal...
>
> This assumes that for a given individual, the columns

I always get confused because the choice of row vs. column
is arbitrary.

What matters is that for each state m there is a simplex
of transition probabilities to each possible next state 1,...,M.

What I was suggesting is that you model the states hierarchically
with a multivariate logistic prior.  That allows for modeling
covariance among the transitions.  For instance, transitions to m1
may be correlated with transitions to m2.

> of the final transition matrix M are i.i.d. following the multinormal distribution.

Not quite --- it's multivariate logistic.  You could
also do multivariate probit by using the probit link
function (cumulative normal Phi).

> Not sure whether this is valid for this particular application. It might well be that the transition probability M[1,2] is correlated with transition probability M[2,3].

Without replicates, there'll be no way to estimate that.  What
I was suggesting has M replicates, one for each state.

Of course, if you have bunches of problems with the same HMM
state structure then you could do it.

Then I think you could generalize to matrix normal distributions,
which I believe Rob's about to add to Stan:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_normal_distribution

> To capture that, one would have to define theta_raw as a vector of length m^2 and evaluate that with a M^2-dimensional multinormal distribution, and then do the softmax transform on each of the m sets of m-length theta_raws.
>
> (Theta_raw needs to be constrained to be positive.)

The point was that theta_raw is unconstrained and each
set of outgoing transition probabilities theta_raw[m] can
be normalized to a simplex softmax(theta_raw[m]).  That induces
a hierarchical structure on the outgoing transitions that allows
correlation between the targets.  You could do the same kind of
thing with the Dirichlet, which gives you mean and variance, but
not covariance.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
My first piece of advice for a large data set and a new model in Stan is to subset the data.  If you have some hierarchical structure stratified subsetting is the way to go to make sure there are some observations per group.  It lets you test the model faster and for some data/prior/model combinations the posterior will be better behaved computationally.  I guess for some models the reverse is true where more data makes it better but it helps to know up-front if you're dealing with one of those.  Once you have something working (converges, reasonable autocorrelation) you can pile on the data and figure out efficiency.  Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
messages.body_plain:
That df+1: at least in earlier versions of Stan, one could have a half-normal but not an artificially truncated normal. I guess it is possible now, but I've stuck to the old habit...

Maybe the prior reflects my prior knowledge. :) Usually there is no reason to assume accurate gaussianity in our applications. I'm not particularly interested in getting the df's or observed variance inferred right. The motivation for t distribution is just to dampen the influence of outliers.

Also my impression has been that the t distribution becomes quite Gaussian around df ≈ 30.  The differences are then mainly further away in the tails, at densities that are astronomically small anyway. But may that isn't so. (I haven't read the papers.)

Then there is the geometry of the parameter space. If in terms of data df≈30 and df≈300 give about the same likelihood, the posterior of the df is long-tailed itself and maybe hard to sample.

Hi, Regarding the model, here are some quick suggestions:
- Instead of using truncated normal for the parameters, could you simply do a normal model on log(alpha) and log(-beta)?  To put it another way, put a normal model on A and B, and then write the A - exp(B)*Z?
- Your model is full of logs and exps which will be slowing you down.  I’m not actually quite sure what’s going on with “inv_cloglog” but I see a log(exp) in your expression.  You are also taking the logs of powers; again, best to just put everything on the log scale so you’re not powering up and logging down all over.
- Ideally with a logistic regression you can use bernoulli_logit; this should be much faster for you.

- If your predictors are discrete, you can bin your 150,000 observations and use the binomal likelihood with one data point per bin

A

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
messages.body_plain:
Aki:
This gamma distribution starts at 0, but usually we assume that the student_t degrees of freedom is at least 1.  Do you add 1 to this gamma distribution, or do you truncate to be greater than 1?
A

> On Mar 6, 2015, at 3:00 AM, Aki Vehtari <Aki.V...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> I recommend as an easy default option
>  nu ~ gamma(2,0.1);
>
> This was proposed and anlysed by Juárez and Steel (2010) (Model-based clustering of non-Gaussian panel data based on skew-t distributions. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 28, 52–66.). Juárez and Steel compere this to Jeffreys prior and report that the difference is small.  Simpson et al (2014) (arXiv:1403.4630) propose a theoretically well justified "penalised complexity (PC) prior", which they show to have a good behavior for the degrees of freedom, too. PC prior might be the best choice, but requires numerical computation of the prior (which could computed in a grid and interpolated etc.). It would be feasible to implement it in Stan, but it would require some work. Unfortunately no-one has compared PC prior and this gamma prior directly, but based on the discussion with Daniel Simpson, although PC prior would be better this gamma(2,0.1) prior is not a bad choice. Thus, I would use it until someone implements the PC prior for degrees of freedom of the Student's t in Stan.
>
> Aki

You can use "gamma" as a parameter name --- there are no conflicts
with variables and function names, or we'd be in big trouble!

You have two problems due to treating Stan like R or JAGS/BUGS
(a not uncommon problem for new users):

1.  you need semicolons at the end of every statement, and

2.  you need to use our function names, e.g., "normal" rather than "dnorm".

It would be possible with some ugly index fiddling for vectorization
and changing basic types to make it faster (see the manual chapter on
arrays vs. matrices and the section on time series model in the regression
chapter), but I'd suggest getting it working first.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Right --- you could use the logit link function instead of inv_cloglog.
We have optimized for that.

>> p[i] <- inv_cloglog(log(census_length[i]) + log(ho) + log(alpha[i] * exp(beta[i] * Z[i])));

>> y ~ bernoulli(p);

would become:

p[i] <- log(census_length[i])
        + log(ho)
        + log(alpha[i])
        + beta[i] * Z[i]);

y ~ bernoulli_logit(p);

I suppose we could write  bernoulli_cloglog at some point, but
I don't know that the inferences are that different from logit.
We also don't have a bernoulli_probit.  Even if you insist
on cloglog for some reason, you want to unwind that log(u * exp(v))
into log(u) + v.

Powering up and logging down is very arithemtically unstable.

I'd also suggest lowering the initial step size and increasing the
target acceptance rate (adapt_delta).  How you do that depends on
the interface.

I would also second Krzysztof's advice --- always start simpler
and build up to the complex model.  Simulate data so you know
you're getting reasonable answers and drop groups if you have to.
You don't want to be debugging and optimizing on a model that
takes 50 minutes and hasn't converged.  Then when you have everything
working, try the bigger data and read a chapter of BDA to relax :-)

The non-centered parameterization (what we used to call the "Matt trick")
is described in the manual.  It's going to be tricky here because
of your parameterization and truncation.

  a0[s] ~ normal(a_GM_grp, a_sd_grp) T[0.0,]; //must be positive

So you can't just do this:

  a0_raw[s] ~ normal(0,1);

  a0[s] <- a_GM_grp * a_sd_grp + a_GM_grp;

It would be possible with some heroic constraint fiddling and
would probably be a win, but I'd try to get this model working first.

We would've named "a_GM_grp" as "mu_a0" and "a_sd_grp"
as "sigma_a0", not that it matters for anything other than making
the models easier for us to read --- your kilometerage may vary.

The other thing you should do to debug is look at the pairs plot for
your parameters --- if there is near perfect correlation between two
variables, you have identifiability problems that will need to be addressed.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2015, at 8:42 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi, Regarding the model, here are some quick suggestions:
> - Instead of using truncated normal for the parameters, could you simply do a normal model on log(alpha) and log(-beta)?  To put it another way, put a normal model on A and B, and then write the A - exp(B)*Z?
> - Your model is full of logs and exps which will be slowing you down.  I’m not actually quite sure what’s going on with “inv_cloglog” but I see a log(exp) in your expression.  You are also taking the logs of powers; again, best to just put everything on the log scale so you’re not powering up and logging down all over.
> - Ideally with a logistic regression you can use bernoulli_logit; this should be much faster for you.
>
> - If your predictors are discrete, you can bin your 150,000 observations and use the binomal likelihood with one data point per bin
>
> A
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob and Andrew, thanks for your advice. I’ll think about what this will mean to the model and give it a go.

Also in trying to explain the maths here I think I found a problem in the original model I posted here. ho should have been included in the log around Z. I've edited it above.

The reason I’m using the complimentary-log-log, loge(− loge(1−p)) link is because it is equivalent to a survival analysis in that coefficients are interpreted as hazard ratios. That is, the hazard for one individual relative to another. It also reduces bias due to long and variable census intervals by allowing census_length to be directly included within the model.

What I am trying to do is fit a competing hazards model using interval-censored data where we don't explicitly know the cause of death but we have a theory that Z may be a primary cause of death and that it's hazard rate will depend on covariates (X1 and X2). As such the overall hazard of an individual, λ, is broken up into two independent hazards λho (z independent death) and λz (z dependent death).

λ(t) = λho(t) + λz(t).

Because I’m dealing with binary (alive/dead) data at variable census lengths I used a cloglog link to model survival as follows:

log(−log(1−Pr(yi,t = 1))) = log(∆t) +log(λho +λz).

This produces a standard competing risks survival function:

S(t) = 1-( -∆t * exp(λho(t)) * exp(λz(t))).

The reason I logged λho +λz is so that each hazard would be treated independently when estimating the overall hazard. This is why I can't simplify the model above to log(a * exp(b)) into log(a) + b. Because it's actually log((a * exp(b)) + ho). Hope this makes some sense…

Also looking forward to your talk on Tuesday Bob!

James

messages.body_plain:
I'd be curious as to how different cloglog and logit are as link
functions---that is to understand your comment about bias.

I do think you can get much more computational efficiency out of the
model by placing at least weakly informative priors on all of the
parameters that currently get improper priors.

Unfortunately, our CDFs are not super efficient nor are they going
to be very computationally stable near boundaries.  And the combination of
distribution plus censoring isn't vectorized.  Your model could
probably be rewritten to vectorize, because the sampling statement

   y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[0,]

is equivalent to:

  y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
  increment_log_prob(log_normal_ccdf(0,mu,sigma));

For N of them, you could do this:

  y ~ normal(mu,sigma);  // vectorizes all N
  increment_log_prob(-N * log_normal_ccdf(0, mu, sigma));

At least I think that's equivalent---you should check my work.

If you have time after the talk on Tuesday, I'd like to sit down
and try to understand your model better.  In particular, I'd like
to understand one well enough to put an example in the manual.
For example, I don't see where you're modeling any kind of censoring.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I should clarify my earlier statement. In survival analysis (as far as I understand it)... the Logit is more appropriate for event times that are truly discrete, while complementary log-log is more appropriate for events that can happen at any time but are only observed to occur in discrete intervals... The latter is the situation that I have.
There is also several differences between the two:
1: unlike the logit function the clog log is asymmetrical. For example, a change from 0.25 to 0.5 on the logit scale is the same as from 0.5 to 0.75. However, on the complementary log-log scale, the difference between probabilities of 0.25 and 0.5 is larger the difference between 0.5 and 0.75.
2: The other difference is that the coefficients of a complementary log-log model have a relative hazards interpretation, just like coefficients from a standard Cox survival model.

In practice, the choice is may not be consequential. So I may be able to use a logit... though I need to better understand the maths since I've included census_length as a hazard adjustor..
The following have several bits of information on the clog log vs logit in survival analysis:
https://books.google.com.au/books?id=RmbZ2y1KLwUC&pg=PA241&lpg=PA241&dq=complementary+log-log+vs+logit+survival+analysis&source=bl&ots=yQ1Z8lDkzH&sig=tXCC_TNHju3lJMcYaxyqGGKDjHE&hl=en&sa=X&ei=N_H6VJvLFZe58gWJrIKQAg&sqi=2&ved=0CDAQ6AEwAw#v=onepage&q=complementary%20log-log%20vs%20logit%20survival%20analysis&f=false

http://www.statisticalhorizons.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/01/Allison_SurvivalAnalysis.pdf
http://www.statpower.net/Content/GCM/Lectures/SW12.pdf
http://data.princeton.edu/pop509/recid3.html

I'm not actually censoring the data here. I'm simply modelling the probability of death between two time steps. I don't have any NA's. The object either was alive or it died.

Happy to catch up Tuesday. Let me know a time.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, March 7, 2015 at 8:15:53 AM UTC-5, James Camac wrote:
> I'm still testing the current model in stan....
> I had to rerun some subsets because my original stan model was slightly parameterised wrong (as mentioned earlier).
> However, using a similar model in JAGS (but without varying alpha and beta) I managed to get it to converge. Though it took about 80,000 iterations.
>
> I'm not too concerned about identifiability issues between ho and Z hazards. It's more whether I'm asking too much from the model to be able to partition X1 and X2 effects on both alpha and beta... and based from my preliminary runs of the model... I think this might be where I'm going to struggle the most.

I guess I didn't catch where the poor identifiability was, but if A+B or A*B is not identifiable, I'd say estimates them as one parameter first to get the model to work on splitting them out once you get over the first hurdle.

>
> Fair point in terms of scaling p^census_length. But wouldn't such a power further diminish computational efficiency as mentioned by Andrew, and as such undo any gain we could get?

I think worrying about computational efficiency when your sampling efficiency is awful is not effective in terms of getting a working model.  First you need to get a good number of effective samples per sample, then you can work on effective samples per second.  I'm not disagreeing about avoiding log(exp(x)) because it's computationally unstable, but avoiding it because it's a little slow won't solve your main problem.

Krzysztof

>
>
> On the plus side fixing the issue with ho (i.e. putting it within the same log as Z) seems to have greatly sped up sampling by approximately 4 fold (from 50 min per 100 iterations to 400 iterations/50 minutes). I'll post up the output tomorrow (midnight here).

>
> I'm guessing if I implement some of the suggestions made here. Particularly on beta and alpha I might be able to further improve this.
>
> I'm really liking stan.. it's quiet intuitive even with the slightly different syntax etc.
>
> On Saturday, 7 March 2015 23:50:01 UTC+11, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > On Saturday, March 7, 2015 at 12:52:04 AM UTC-5, James Camac wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Bob and Andrew, thanks for your advice. I’ll think about what this will mean to the model and give it a go.
> > >
> > > Also in trying to explain the maths here I think I found a problem in the original model I posted here. ho should have been included in the log around Z. I've edited it above.
> > >
> > > The reason I’m using the complimentary-log-log, loge(− loge(1−p)) link is because it is equivalent to a survival analysis in that coefficients are interpreted as hazard ratios. That is, the hazard for one individual relative to another. It also reduces bias due to long and variable census intervals by allowing census_length to be directly included within the model.
> > I can see wanting to go with the relative hazard interpretation but you can include census length by scaling p afterwards, something like p^census_length, that works regardless of link function.
> >
> > >
> > > What I am trying to do is fit a competing hazards model using interval-censored data where we don't explicitly know the cause of death but we have a theory that Z may be a primary cause of death and that it's hazard rate will depend on covariates (X1 and X2). As such the overall hazard of an individual, λ, is broken up into two independent hazards λho (z independent death) and λz (z dependent death).
> > >
> > > λ(t) = λho(t) + λz(t).
> > >
> > > Because I’m dealing with binary (alive/dead) data at variable census lengths I used a cloglog link to model survival as follows:
> > >
> > > log(−log(1−Pr(yi,t = 1))) = log(∆t) +log(λho +λz).
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > This produces a standard competing risks survival function:
> > >
> > > S(t) = 1-( -∆t * exp(λho(t)) * exp(λz(t))).
> > You didn't mention if you got a model with a single hazard working? If you haven't yet that might be much easier for trouble shooting (since it avoids the whole identifiability issue).
> >
> >  Krzysztof
> >
> > >
> > >
> > > The reason I logged λho +λz is so that each hazard would be treated independently when estimating the overall hazard. This is why I can't simplify the model above to log(a * exp(b)) into log(a) + b. Because it's actually log((a * exp(b)) + ho). Hope this makes some sense…
> > >
> > > Also looking forward to your talk on Tuesday Bob!
> > >
> > > James

(a) It doesn’t seem right to me that users should be routinely manipulating the step sizes.  This is the sort of thing that Stan should do automatically.

(b) I’m not talking about smaller data (although, sure, that’s a good idea). I’m talking about cleaning up the model.  The original model as written was full of inefficiency.  Again, I don’t think it makes sense _at all_ for users to be playing with the internals until they first get the model to make sense.

> really get it right with large step sizes.  But I take your
> point --- it's best to start with smaller data that won't need
> so much fiddling.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Mar 7, 2015, at 3:21 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Bob

>> A

Krzysztof,
I know what you’re saying, but sometimes a rewrite of the model to be computationally cleaner, can also motivate a change in the model itself.  In practice, the “model” that’s written is not fixed in stone, it itself is a construction.  And, once the model is written more clearly, we can often construct it better.
To put it another way:  the Folk Theorem.
A

> On Mar 8, 2015, at 8:03 AM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> (a) It doesn’t seem right to me that users should be routinely manipulating the step sizes.  This is the sort of thing that Stan should do automatically.
>

Agreed.  Any ideas on how to make that happen without sacrificing
a lot of efficiency for the bulk of our models?  We could start with
lower step sizes, but that would slow down the not-so-complex models.

Concretely, do you think it'd be worth it to, say, slow down
warmup by a factor of 2 in order to add robustness for complex models?

We have the chicken-and-egg problem of needing to adapt to find good
step sizes and mass matrices, and vice versa.

The big problem is that we don't know how many steps are enough to adapt.
With lots of computing power, we could try various things, see how they
do, and choose the best.  Either one at a time or in parallel.

Unlike Metropolis for roughly multivariate normal priors, there's not
an ideal universal target acceptance rate for HMC/NUTS (see Betancourt
and Girolami's hierarchical modeling paper for details).  [I know you
know this, Andrew, I'm just including the ref because this is going out
to stan-users.]

> (b) I’m not talking about smaller data (although, sure, that’s a good idea). I’m talking about cleaning up the model.  The original model as written was full of inefficiency.  Again, I don’t think it makes sense _at all_ for users to be playing with the internals until they first get the model to make sense.

By the same argument, this is all stuff Stan should be doing internally.
There's no reason in principle we can't figure out all these transforms
on our own and carry them out through program analysis and optimized
code generation.

But we're nowhere near there yet.

- Bob
