messages.body_plain:
The error message is telling you that your problem is that
the sigma argument is a 2D array.

First off, the reason the patched version is "desperately slow"
is that you're oversampling:

  // The following works, but is desperately slow:
  // for (n in 1:N)
  //   for (k in 1:K)
  //     RHG[n] ~ normal(rnd_slope + gamma[n,k]*herb[n], sigma); you can change this:

That should presumably be RHG[n,k] ~ ...

As is, you're doing K times too much work here and also providing
the wrong distribution.  Unfortunately, there's no way for us to
auto-detect this problem and allow vectorization.

To make things efficient, you need to rearrange your data.

The right thing to do differs as to whether N >> K or vice versa.
I'll just do it the easy way, including making the variable
declarations more efficient without changing how the I/O works (see
the chapter on arrays vs. matrices for details of why this is better):

  vector[K] RHG[N]; //  matrix for RHGs

  vector[K] gamma[N]; // coefficient for herbivore

  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma[N]; // stochastic effects

  for (n in 1:N)

    RHG[n] ~ normal(rnd_slope + gamma[n] * herb[n], sigma[n]);

This will work because

    RHG[n]    : vector[K]
    rnd_slope : vector[K]
    gamma[n]  : vector[K]
    herb[n]   : real

If N >> K, it would make sense to transpose all this and vectorize
in a for (k in 1:K) loop, but I don't have the stamina to work it
all out for you.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Maybe this is just me being over-cautious about it but I would not try to brute-force it from here.  I think those n_eff numbers are charitable which means it could run for a few days and you would still have a limited few samples from the posterior.  It looks like a_GM_spp is bumping up against its zero boundary and there must be some outlier groups because the scale is around 4.  b_GM_spp is hugely negative which is making that whole term go to zero so the posterior has to become insensitive to whatever happens to alpha (so without priors alpha is just wandering around lost).  Maybe this model needs a way of informing you that the alpha * exp(beta) term is not important without getting lost (so at least weak priors on b_gm_grp, b_sd_grp, b1) but at that point you might as well go through the trouble of doing priors on everything.  That's all I can tell from the trace plots.

Hope that helps.... it's interesting to see this since I have one of these models with log(exp(a+log(b))) things in my near future... (joking, but only sort of).

Krzysztof

Hi Krzysztof, I think you and Bob may be right.. putting weakly informative priors on everything may help.
I'll set priors on a_GM_grp, b_GM_grp, a1,a2, b1 and b2 the sigmas... but which type of prior do you recommend? Cauchy priors ( & half cauchy for sigmas)?

Also I've been thinking more about the truncation around a0 (a0[s] ~ normal(a_GM_spp, a_sd_spp) T[0.0,]). I guess it can technically be negative as long as alpha is never greater than ho (i.e. the overall hazard must always positive).  So maybe I can get rid of that truncation...
As for b0... current evidence suggests that it should be negative and as such the truncation is a form of informative prior.

Lastly, the model I describe above is a log((exp...) + ho) which I don't think can be simplified.

I have to admit I don't fully understand the 'under the hood' workings of HMC or how the code should be written to optimise it's geometry. Or exactly how changing the step size will help/not help.
> >

messages.body_plain:
Truncated distributions aren’t necessarily wrong, and they can work fine as priors.  But as a model for data or for a group of parameters, a truncated model has the odd property that it can have a high probability of being very close to 0 on one side, while being impossible to be close to 0 on the other.  It depends on the context but often this doesn’t quite make sense.

El domingo, 8 de marzo de 2015, 2:42:16 (UTC+1), Bob Carpenter escribió:
> The error message is telling you that your problem is that
> the sigma argument is a 2D array.
>
> First off, the reason the patched version is "desperately slow"
> is that you're oversampling:
>
>   // The following works, but is desperately slow:
>   // for (n in 1:N)
>   //   for (k in 1:K)
>   //     RHG[n] ~ normal(rnd_slope + gamma[n,k]*herb[n], sigma); you can change this:
>
> That should presumably be RHG[n,k] ~ ...
>
> As is, you're doing K times too much work here and also providing
> the wrong distribution.  Unfortunately, there's no way for us to
> auto-detect this problem and allow vectorization.
>
> To make things efficient, you need to rearrange your data.
>
> The right thing to do differs as to whether N >> K or vice versa.
> I'll just do it the easy way, including making the variable
> declarations more efficient without changing how the I/O works (see
> the chapter on arrays vs. matrices for details of why this is better):
>
>   vector[K] RHG[N]; //  matrix for RHGs
>
>   vector[K] gamma[N]; // coefficient for herbivore
>
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma[N]; // stochastic effects
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     RHG[n] ~ normal(rnd_slope + gamma[n] * herb[n], sigma[n]);
>
> This will work because
>
>     RHG[n]    : vector[K]
>     rnd_slope : vector[K]
>     gamma[n]  : vector[K]
>     herb[n]   : real
>
> If N >> K, it would make sense to transpose all this and vectorize
> in a for (k in 1:K) loop, but I don't have the stamina to work it
> all out for you.
>
> - Bob

A typical problem with truncated distributions is that
the truncation was done on a guess and the real value
lies near or beyond a boundary.  In that case, you'll see
the samples bunching up near a boundary.

For instance, if the real data is normal(0,100), and you model
with normal(mu,sigma), where sigma is constrained to lie in (0,20),
as we see in some user models, then the estimates are going to bunch
up near 20, when they should be allowed to be larger.  This is why
we'd prefer a soft constraint.  But a hard enough soft constraint
can have the same problem if there's not much data.

On the other hand, if you have a physical constraint implying
truncation, or are using a distribution that's trunctated (e.g.,
positive like a gamma distribution), then you have to define
constrained variables in Stan.  And if you have a scale parameter
like sigma above, it absolute must be constrained to be above 0.
Anything else will just lead to rejections and failures to initialize.

- Bob

It adds curvature around the point you expect the answer to be.
It's hard to negotiate big flat areas.

>> I'll set priors on a_GM_grp, b_GM_grp, a1,a2, b1 and b2 the sigmas... but which type of prior do you recommend? Cauchy priors ( & half cauchy for sigmas)?
>>
>> Also I've been thinking more about the truncation around a0 (a0[s] ~ normal(a_GM_spp, a_sd_spp) T[0.0,]). I guess it can technically be negative as long as alpha is never greater than ho (i.e. the overall hazard must always positive).

One way to do this is with an exp transform as in a GLM
model for a Poisson's mean.  You can add constraints
so that (alpha < ho).

>> So maybe I can get rid of that truncation...
>> As for b0... current evidence suggests that it should be negative and as such the truncation is a form of informative prior.

This is the kind of thing we'd inform against --- if the
data makes it negative, it'll be negative.  A zero upper
bound does a -log(x) transform, which stretches out the
space near zero, and can make the scales hard for the
sampler negotiate (it has to move further and further as
it gets near zero.

>> Lastly, the model I describe above is a log((exp...) + ho) which I don't think can be simplified.

If you've got an exp inside a log, it can be simplified algebraically
and made more arithmetically stable.  Check out the log_sum_exp operation.

log(exp(a) + b) should be coded as log_sum_exp(a, log(b)) for stability.
The problem si that exp(a) will underflow/overflow if a is outside of
(-700,700) or so, but the log_sum_exp form will never underflow or overflow.

>> I have to admit I don't fully understand the 'under the hood' workings of HMC or how the code should be written to optimise it's geometry. Or exactly how changing the step size will help/not help.

The key is thinking about the transformed-to-unconstrainedn space
and that you're moving in it with a discrete step size guided by
the gradient of the -log prob on the unconstrained scale.  The manual
has a chapter laying out all the transforms.

- Bob

P.S.  Our n_eff estimates are pretty conservative if you're
running multiple chains from diffuse starting points.

messages.body_plain:
I'm going to try to clarify the question first.  Suppose
your data looks like this:

  vector[N] y[K];
  vector[N] x[K];

and parameters you want to estimate are:

  real beta[K];
  real sigma[K];

You should get the same posterior for each beta[k]
and sigma[k] if you have a single Stan program with
likelihood:

  for (k in 1:K) {
    y[k] ~ normal(beta[k] * x[k], sigma[k]);
    beta[k] ~ ... some prior ...
    sigma[k] ~ .. some prior ...
  }

or if you run K separate instances of Stan with
likelihood

  y[k] ~ normal(beta[k] * x[k], sigma[k];
  beta[k] ~ ... some prior ...
  sigma[k] ~ .. some prior ...

Now if you provide a hierarchical prior things will be
different, which I'd strongly advise if the K instances
are exchangeable.

- Bob

> You don’t.
>
> When you marginalize out over the mixture components you’re assigning at least some prior
> probability to each component which can never be forced exactly to zero.  A proper Bayesian
> analysis never makes a hard decision to exclude components so there is no canonical way
> of trying to impose a “significance” threshold.  You have to define a criteria for defining one
> yourself.
>
> For example, one criteria might be that for a mixture component to be excluded the posterior
> must shrink towards zero relative to the prior.  Of course how you define “shrink” and “shrink
> enough to be excluded” are open questions.

increment_log_prob(x) just adds x to the result of the log
probability function.

It's probably log_sum_exp that is the problem.  Just expand
the definitions out and look at your density --- that's not
a Bayesian issue --- it works the same way if you're doing
optimization for penalized maximum likelihood.

The hard constraint on alpha does not look good to me.  I prefer a prior such as normal.  Also I’m guessing that instead of that “reflect” thing, you could use an ordered data type in Stan and that would work better.
A

> On Mar 10, 2015, at 2:57 PM, Thomas <daub...@tcd.ie> wrote:
>

> After experimenting a good deal with the above model, I have for now settled on the following specification (see code below):
>
> - pin down one of the term/item parameters each, draw the rest from a bivariate normal, with mean zero, using the Cholesky factor re-parameterization, using a non-hierarchical prior on the covariance matrix (3s on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere)
> - keep the soft constraint on the ideal points using the standard normal prior
> - resolve the reflection invariance only in the generated quantities block
>
> This works well and the Rhats generally look good after a few hundred iterations (from random inits), and I can replicate the means I get from an ML version of the model. However, there is high autocorrelation in the chains, the effective sample sizes are well below a third of the number of iterations for many parameters, and the warmup seems slow (for a 350x55 cells table, 200 warmup iterations take something between 2 and 4 mins, sampling itself is quicker, that's on a 3.6 Ghz machine with 16 GB RAM).
> Ok, I understand that the merely soft constraint on the ideal points leads to shifts in other parameters across draws, but e.g. using an additional hard sum-to-zero constraint on the ideal points only somewhat alleviates the problem (I've also read the post on STZ constraints, where it was argued that hard constraints do not essentially change the model.)
>
> Is there anything wrong with the code, is it just the nature of the model, or is there anything else I can try to do? Does the thinning interval choice actually affect the warmup behavior - I guess not?
> Please let me know if you need further information about the model or its behavior.
>
> Thanks for any hints!
>
> Thomas
>
> data {
> int<lower=1> D; // number of docs
> int<lower=1> T; // number of terms/cats
> int<lower=1> N; // number of obs = number of docs * number of cats
> int<lower=1> doc[N]; // doc id
> int<lower=1> term[N]; // cat id
> int<lower=0> y[N]; // counts as one long vector
> cov_matrix[2] Sigma_termpar; // prior for co-variance matrix
>
> transformed data {
> matrix[2,2] L;
> L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_termpar);
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector<lower=-20, upper=20>[D] alpha;
> matrix[T-1,2] termpar_e;
> vector[D] theta_raw;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> matrix[T,2] termpar_raw;
>
> // constrain first termpar pair to 0; and remaining termpar ~ multi_normal(0,Sigma_termpar)
> termpar_raw <- append_row(rep_row_vector(0,2), termpar_e*L);
> }
>
> model {
>
> vector[N] logmu;
> // note: alpha is uniform
> to_vector(termpar_e) ~ normal(0,1);
> theta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
>
> for(n in 1:N){
> logmu[n] <- alpha[doc[n]] + termpar_raw[term[n],1] + theta_raw[doc[n]] * termpar_raw[term[n],2];
> }
> y ~ poisson_log(logmu);
> }
>
> generated quantities {
> vector[D] theta;
> matrix[T,2] termpar;
> real reflect;
>
> reflect <- if_else(theta_raw[1] > theta_raw[2],-1,1);
> for(t in 1:T) {
> termpar[t] <- to_row_vector(termpar_raw[t]);
> termpar[t,2] <- reflect*termpar[t,2];
> }
> theta <- reflect*theta_raw;
> }
>
> On Thursday, October 9, 2014 at 9:41:40 PM UTC+2, Thomas wrote:
> > Thanks very much for the rapid reply, Bob!
> >
> > Regarding the half-normal priors: Yes, I constrained one beta to be positive in some earlier versions of the model. What sometimes happened was that this beta then was estimated as barely larger than zero (although it was one of the more discriminating ones in the unconstrained version), and the scale was still in the wrong direction.

> > > >
> > > > As constraints, one psi and one beta are set to zero, and the ideal points theta receive a standard normal prior. A conditional statement based on the order of two betas is used to reverse the scale when necessary (I know that half-normal priors might be better for that, but I had mixed experiences when working with those).
> > >
> > > I'm curious what the mixed experience was.  Did you
> > > constrain the parameters to be positive?  The log transform on the
> > > variables does change the posterior geometry and hence affects
> > > sampling.
> > >
> > > > It seems that the constraints are sufficient to identify the model, at least I get very similar results across different runs.
> > >
> > > That does sound sufficient to identify the model.
> > >
> > > > It seems to work since the standard normal prior on the ideal points theta apparently leads to a standard normal posterior distribution of the ideal points. Is there a simple answer why this happens?
> > >
> > > Yes.  When you have too many degrees of freedom in the parameterization (i.e.,
> > > non-identifiability), what happens is that one parameter can go up
> > > or down in scale or shift in location, with a corresponding shift or scaling
> > > of another parameter group without affecting the posterior
> > > density.   By assigning one group of variables a normal(0,1) prior, that
> > > identifies the scale and location that's going to fit best, hence you
> > > get normal(0,1) posteriors for the constrained variable and everything else
> > > floats.
> > >
> > > There's a discussion in the Gelman and Hill's book section on (multilevel)
> > > IRT and ideal-point models.
> > >
> > > > I would not necessarily have expected that, and when I code the same model in Jags, theta does not come out standardized in the posterior and the model lacks identification.
> > >
> > > My guess would be that either (a) it's not exactly the same model in
> > > JAGS, or (b) you haven't run JAGS long enough to converge.
> > > Gibbs sampling is slow to converge if you have correlations in the posterior,
> > > as you do in these essentially unidentified models.
> > >
> > > > Is it ok to rely on the prior doing the job in Stan or would it still be better to standardize the ideal points deterministically (probably at the expense of speed?)? Any hints appreciated.
> > >
> > > It is critical to rely on the prior or another means of
> > > identification of the model in Stan.  Just standardizing the
> > > resulting parameter draws won't work.  There's a discussion
> > > of the issue for a very simple example with posterior draws
> > > in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual, with
> > > more explanation about what's going on and why the post-standardization
> > > seems to work in Gibbs (as far as I know, nobody's shown it gives
> > > the right answer formally, though Andrew's convinced it does), but
> > > not in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
> > >
> > > - Bob

What's an "ML version of the model"?  You mean software
to fit a point estimate?

If you only want a posterior mode, you can use Stan's
optimization functionality.

And you absolutely don't want to do a signum-type
reflection if it leads to different posterior modes.  For
Stan to be efficient, the parameters themselves should be
identified.

My request is to have a "silent_reject()" function so that I don't get thousands of lines of the same message.

Thanks,
Cameron

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much for the suggestions, Andrew and Bob!

(Yes, I used some ML code outside of stan to compare it to my posterior means - but I'd like to get the Bayesian version working.)

I replaced the uniform on alpha with a normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha) and that makes it run somewhat faster.

I tried the ordered vector suggestion for the reflection invariance, but that doesn't work since the two constrained ideal points may end up being placed very close together (that's similar to what happens when using two half-normals).

I am aware that the above version does not actually solve the bimodality in the model. Alternatively, I have also tried pinning down two ideal points to fix the direction, but I am struggling with achieving that the constraints bite, i.e. that the remaining ideal points are placed relative to the two fixed ones.
If I fix two positions known to be quite extreme to -1 and 1, and I use a normal(0,5) prior or a hierarchical normal prior (mu_theta,sigma_theta) for the others, then the polarity of the remaining ideal points can still vary across chains: as compensation, the rows with the two constrained thetas just get two alphas that are "off" (when I compare them across chains).  I may be wrong, but I guess another problem in choosing the prior for the unconstrained ideal points is the multiplicative indeterminacy between the ideal points and the discrimination parameters. In my original model, the standard normal prior on the ideal points pretty much fixes their variance and the discrimnations adjust (but the direction is not fixed). When pinning down two ideal points, the direction is fixed, but it is a rather weak constraint on the variance of the ideal points (which still needs to be inferred), and that makes it also harder to infer the variance of the discriminations at the same time.
Any suggestions on what priors to use on the remaining ideal points if I fix two? What looks most promising so far is a normal(0, sigma_theta), but I need to test it further.

Thanks!

On Wednesday, 11 March 2015 00:24:18 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What's an "ML version of the model"?  You mean software
> to fit a point estimate?
>
> If you only want a posterior mode, you can use Stan's
> optimization functionality.
>
> And you absolutely don't want to do a signum-type
> reflection if it leads to different posterior modes.  For
> Stan to be efficient, the parameters themselves should be
> identified.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Mar 11, 2015, at 5:57 AM, Thomas <daub...@tcd.ie> wrote:
> >
> > After experimenting a good deal with the above model, I have for now settled on the following specification (see code below):
> >
> > - pin down one of the term/item parameters each, draw the rest from a bivariate normal, with mean zero, using the Cholesky factor re-parameterization, using a non-hierarchical prior on the covariance matrix (3s on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere)
> > - keep the soft constraint on the ideal points using the standard normal prior
> > - resolve the reflection invariance only in the generated quantities block
> >
> > This works well and the Rhats generally look good after a few hundred iterations (from random inits), and I can replicate the means I get from an ML version of the model. However, there is high autocorrelation in the chains, the effective sample sizes are well below a third of the number of iterations for many parameters, and the warmup seems slow (for a 350x55 cells table, 200 warmup iterations take something between 2 and 4 mins, sampling itself is quicker, that's on a 3.6 Ghz machine with 16 GB RAM).
> > Ok, I understand that the merely soft constraint on the ideal points leads to shifts in other parameters across draws, but e.g. using an additional hard sum-to-zero constraint on the ideal points only somewhat alleviates the problem (I've also read the post on STZ constraints, where it was argued that hard constraints do not essentially change the model.)
> >
> > Is there anything wrong with the code, is it just the nature of the model, or is there anything else I can try to do? Does the thinning interval choice actually affect the warmup behavior - I guess not?
> > Please let me know if you need further information about the model or its behavior.
> >
> > Thanks for any hints!
> >
> > Thomas
> >
> > data {
> > int<lower=1> D; // number of docs
> > int<lower=1> T; // number of terms/cats
> > int<lower=1> N; // number of obs = number of docs * number of cats
> > int<lower=1> doc[N]; // doc id
> > int<lower=1> term[N]; // cat id
> > int<lower=0> y[N]; // counts as one long vector
> > cov_matrix[2] Sigma_termpar; // prior for co-variance matrix
> >
> > transformed data {
> > matrix[2,2] L;
> > L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_termpar);
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> > vector<lower=-20, upper=20>[D] alpha;
> > matrix[T-1,2] termpar_e;
> > vector[D] theta_raw;
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> > matrix[T,2] termpar_raw;
> >
> > // constrain first termpar pair to 0; and remaining termpar ~ multi_normal(0,Sigma_termpar)
> > termpar_raw <- append_row(rep_row_vector(0,2), termpar_e*L);
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >
> > vector[N] logmu;
> > // note: alpha is uniform
> > to_vector(termpar_e) ~ normal(0,1);
> > theta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
> >
> > for(n in 1:N){
> > logmu[n] <- alpha[doc[n]] + termpar_raw[term[n],1] + theta_raw[doc[n]] * termpar_raw[term[n],2];
> > }
> > y ~ poisson_log(logmu);
> > }
> >
> > generated quantities {
> > vector[D] theta;
> > matrix[T,2] termpar;
> > real reflect;
> >
> > reflect <- if_else(theta_raw[1] > theta_raw[2],-1,1);
> > for(t in 1:T) {
> > termpar[t] <- to_row_vector(termpar_raw[t]);
> > termpar[t,2] <- reflect*termpar[t,2];
> > }
> > theta <- reflect*theta_raw;
> > }
> >
> > On Thursday, October 9, 2014 at 9:41:40 PM UTC+2, Thomas wrote:
> > Thanks very much for the rapid reply, Bob!
> >
> > Regarding the half-normal priors: Yes, I constrained one beta to be positive in some earlier versions of the model. What sometimes happened was that this beta then was estimated as barely larger than zero (although it was one of the more discriminating ones in the unconstrained version), and the scale was still in the wrong direction.
> >
> > On 9 October 2014 21:17, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Oct 9, 2014, at 2:42 PM, Thomas <daub...@tcd.ie> wrote:
> >
> > > I'm fitting a multinomial (by means of Poisson) IRT/ideal point model for category counts in policy documents with
> > >
> > > Count(document, category) ~ Poisson(exp(alpha_doc + psi_cat + beta_cat*theta_doc))
> > >
> > > As constraints, one psi and one beta are set to zero, and the ideal points theta receive a standard normal prior. A conditional statement based on the order of two betas is used to reverse the scale when necessary (I know that half-normal priors might be better for that, but I had mixed experiences when working with those).
> >
> > I'm curious what the mixed experience was.  Did you
> > constrain the parameters to be positive?  The log transform on the
> > variables does change the posterior geometry and hence affects
> > sampling.
> >
> > > It seems that the constraints are sufficient to identify the model, at least I get very similar results across different runs.
> >
> > That does sound sufficient to identify the model.
> >
> > > It seems to work since the standard normal prior on the ideal points theta apparently leads to a standard normal posterior distribution of the ideal points. Is there a simple answer why this happens?
> >
> > Yes.  When you have too many degrees of freedom in the parameterization (i.e.,
> > non-identifiability), what happens is that one parameter can go up
> > or down in scale or shift in location, with a corresponding shift or scaling
> > of another parameter group without affecting the posterior
> > density.   By assigning one group of variables a normal(0,1) prior, that
> > identifies the scale and location that's going to fit best, hence you
> > get normal(0,1) posteriors for the constrained variable and everything else
> > floats.
> >
> > There's a discussion in the Gelman and Hill's book section on (multilevel)
> > IRT and ideal-point models.
> >
> > > I would not necessarily have expected that, and when I code the same model in Jags, theta does not come out standardized in the posterior and the model lacks identification.
> >
> > My guess would be that either (a) it's not exactly the same model in
> > JAGS, or (b) you haven't run JAGS long enough to converge.
> > Gibbs sampling is slow to converge if you have correlations in the posterior,
> > as you do in these essentially unidentified models.
> >
> > > Is it ok to rely on the prior doing the job in Stan or would it still be better to standardize the ideal points deterministically (probably at the expense of speed?)? Any hints appreciated.
> >
> > It is critical to rely on the prior or another means of
> > identification of the model in Stan.  Just standardizing the
> > resulting parameter draws won't work.  There's a discussion
> > of the issue for a very simple example with posterior draws
> > in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual, with
> > more explanation about what's going on and why the post-standardization
> > seems to work in Gibbs (as far as I know, nobody's shown it gives
> > the right answer formally, though Andrew's convinced it does), but
> > not in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
> >
> > - Bob

messages.subject: Bayesian identification using ordered priors
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian identification using ordered priors
messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 11, 2015, at 2:13 PM, Thomas <daub...@tcd.ie> wrote:
>
> I tried the ordered vector suggestion for the reflection invariance, but that doesn’t work since the two constrained ideal points may end up being placed very close together (that's similar to what happens when using two half-normals).

The ordering should work even if the two points are close.  But if that is a concern (that you don’t want to constrain them to be ordered), you can simply give them different priors with equal variances but with one prior having a mean lower than the other.  This should break the aliasing and identify the model.  In general we much prefer this sort of identification strategy, (rather than having an unidentified model and then summing to average over aliases).

Bob,

Sorry - it is quite far back in the thread. Just to copy my (pseudo) explanation of the generative process from earlier:
"Imagine a lane. On the lane, there are different obstacles, varying in size (getting larger as one moves down the lane). Now along comes two components A and B, which are physically connected. They move down the lane until they cannot proceed any further due to obstacles. Next comes A and C, which are also physically connected. C is, however, slightly smaller than B, and the A-C component can move further down the lane. The number A-B and A-C are typically in the millions, and what we count is not the actual number of A-B components, but A and B individually (typically these are in millions++, so we use the log(count+1) transformation). Not all of the components stops the exact same place (hence they have a profile).”

My initial idea was to use a mixture model (with a dirichlet process prior for the mixture - in this case just a reasonable high number of mixtures) to estimate which components came from the same mixture. That is, identify A-B and A-C as physically connected. My question was, what is the most convenient way in stan to get the probability of each sample, feature (x[n,m) being in mixture 1 .. K. Normally I would just compute the density under the estimated gaussian distribution, but I am not quite sure what is the most optimal way to do this in Stan.

Using those probabilities, my (very naive) idea to estimate which components come from the same mixture would simply be to apply some lower cutoff, and if the probability exceeds that they are from the same mixture. Following this, then simply just identify which components have the same active mixture(s). But again, this is a very naive idea. You suggested a HMM instead. I am not quite sure how I would apply a HMM in this case. I guess another approach could also be to construct a binary matrix. I.e. b[n,m] == 1 if the mixture is active, otherwise zero, and then apply some latent allocation procedure.

Sorry for the broken link! https://gist.github.com/demodw/dec9724b96fbf8f8e428 is the correct one.

Cheers,
David

Thanks --- I remember now.  Though I probably don't understand
the problem well enough to be of much help.

What are the numbers in y[n]?  I didn't understand what the A, B,
and C were or what was observed.

You didn't even declare y in the
gist, so it can't possibly compile.

The model you have (modulo not defining y) is just a standard
mixture of K normals.

If you want to approximate a Dirichlet process, you have to
let the Dirichlet basis alpha shrink to alpha/K as you increase
K.  At least I'm pretty sure that's how it'd work, though I have
no idea if it'll work in Stan.

Do you really think there will be 1000 mixture components?  It's
likely to lead to very slow going and potentially arithmetic instability.

Yes, it's a good idea to put a prior on everything.  Choose something
consistent with what you expect the posterior to be given your
knowledge of the problem and the scale of the variables involved.

If your data's all positive, normal can still be a good approximation.
For example, it's a good approximation of a binomial as the number
of observations grows (just the central limit theorem).  And in that
case, you wouldn't want to log transform the counts.

- Bob

The problem is explained a bit more in scientific jargon in the introduction of http://bioinformatics.oxfordjournals.org/content/early/2014/10/08/bioinformatics.btu623.full.pdf+html (paywall’ed). Sorry, I usually don’t make this many mistakes when copy/pasting. y is a vector[M] y[N] (https://gist.github.com/demodw/8a3f0963b7b2cad36508). A, B and C are physical entities (proteins), that are observed to co-migrate.

Technically the numbers in y are counts. But the counts are in the billions (I actually suspect Stan is overflowing when I feed the numbers — it gives mysterious errors that does not occur when I log2 transform the data). The log2 values typically range between 20-50.

1,000 is a somewhat conservative estimate. It is indeed very slow when working with the full data, and identifiability across chains is a big problem. I’m wondering if using a EM optimisation is better in this situation, given the large number of mixtures.

messages.body_plain:
There's no built-in way to do that.  You have to write
the loops yourself.  If you want to get rid of row and
column n in an N x N matrix, then you can do it one
quadrant at a time, as so:

matrix delete_row_col(matrix a, int n) {
  matrix[rows(a) - 1, cols(a) - 1] result;
  for (i in 1:(n-1)) {
    for (j in 1:(n-1))
      result[i,j] <- a[i,j];
    for (j in (n+1):N)
      result[i,j-1] <- a[i,j];
  }
  for (i in (n+1):N) {
    for (j in 1:(n-1))
      result[i-1,j] <- a[i,j];
    for (j in (n+1):N)
      result[i-1,j-1] <- a[i,j];
  }
  return result;
}

Of course, if you don't know the row/col, then you need to write
another loop to find that first.  And if you have more than one match,
then the function gets trickier, but you could reduce it to removing
one at a time.

- Bob

> it's not broken down into standard statistical terminology.

That is understandable.

>
> So my question is:  what are the entries in the y[n] vectors for n in 1:N?
> How big is N that you want 1000 mixtures?
>
> If they're counts, what are they counts of?  I can't connect the dots between
> counts and migrating proteins.  I'm guessing that you have N different
> proteins, M places they can get stuck in an experiment, and y[n] represents
> the counts of the places they get stuck over billions of replications for each
> n in 1:N.  So sum(y[n]) is in the billions, but how big is N and how big is M?

Yes, exactly. Except y[n] is is not the count of the places, but the count of the number of proteins in a particular place. In figure 1a from the paper, there are 60 such places. In each of the 60 places, there are either 0 proteins (the protein is not found in the given place or could not be detected), or a number in the billions if the protein is present. Each y[n] thus holds a vector of counts for the given place, so that y[n,m] is the count of protein n in place m.

>
> And the goal's then to cluster the proteins by the distributions of where
> they get stuck?  To what end?  Are you sure you want to run a Bayesian
> model here?

What we want to identify are the proteins that has the same profile / is drawn from the same mixture. If two proteins are co-migrating, they are most likely physically interacting in a complex. At least that is what we hypothesise. The idea running the Bayesian model would be to have priors on the number of mixtures, as well as infer which proteins are co-migrating. It could be there are better ways of doing it, but our initial thought was the Bayesian framework as it is quite flexible.

>
> I don't see how regression is related to clustering.

Definitely, it is not. It was just another approach used in a prior paper.

Cheers,
David

Thanks --- now I get it.

So what I'd do from a Bayesian perspective is calculate the posterior
probability that two proteins, indexed n and n', are from the same
cluster given the observed data, i.e.,

  Pr[protein[n] drawn from same cluster as protein[n'] | y]

You can do this with Stan.

The basic idea is that you have the mixture model you have, but
use a lognormal if you are going to log transform, then calculate
the above event probabilities in the generated quantities block:

generated quantities {
  matrix[N,N] Pr_same_cluster;

  for (m in 1:N)
    for (n in (n+1):N)
      Pr_same_cluster[m,n] <- pr_same(m,n,y,theta,mu,sigma);
}

you use for the mixture,

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure what you mean.  Positions (indexes?) in
matrices aren't real numbers.

You're right that Stan does not automatically demote reals
to integers --- in that way it's like Java, not like C/C++.

> For instance, imagine you have a 4 by 4 matrix
> >
> >       | 1 2 1 1 |
> > A = | 2 8 2 2 |
> >       | 3 2 3 3 |
> >       | 4 2 4 4 |
> >
> > and you want to delete the row and column of the element 8, i.e., delete the second row and the second column.

Assuming this example reflects what you want to do, you
need to write a function to find the index:

  int diagonal_index_of(matrix x, real y) {
    for (i in 1:rows(x))
      if (x[i,i] == y) return i;
    return -1;
  }

Then just plug the index into the other function.  Or put
them together into a single function.

- Bob

Slow in what respect?  The only meaningful comparison is ESS/time.
or time/ESS.  In general Stan tends to be slower per _iteration_ but
much, much faster in ESS/time.  Also have you verified that each
algorithm is giving results consistent with the true values used to
simulate the data?

That said, one immediate problem with your model is that <lower=0>
already guarantees that all of your parameters will be positive so you
don’t need to do those exponentials in the transformed parameters
block (right now you’re essentially doing exp(exp(log(x)) = exp(x)!).
Those gamma priors are notoriously dangerous (they can cause
awkward posteriors that can bias sampling and it’s hard to see the
problems in WinBUGS) and there a few more optimizations that can
be made, but see if fixing double-exponential makes a huge difference
first.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been trying to fit some reading/reaction time (rt) data with a shifted log normal hierarchical model, where the shift also varies by subject. We (in psycholinguistics) usually use linear mixed models with lmer (from lme4 R package) and we either use log(rt) or (1/rt) as the dependent variable (to have it "normally distributed") and I would like to know if it's justified to fit a shifted-lognormal dist.

So I built the model using Sorensen & Vasishth's tutorial and I followed Bob Carpenter's post <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/zEKVSv6_K70/AaMIZg0m5S8J> for the log-shifted part . And I added shifts by subject.

First of all, when I compile the model I get the following, which I understood from Bob's post, that I can safely ignore:

Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) contains a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
 You must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
  Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
    subtract(rt,c) ~ lognormal_log(...)

And then during the sampling, I get a bunch of these ones:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::lognormal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable[475]  is -0.450891:0, but must be >= 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I guess that's because the general shift + shift by subject is lower than 0 in some of the iterations. But the model converges anyway, so the first question is: can I ignore the errors? Or should I fix this? and how? Should I force the by-subj shift to be not smaller than -shift and not bigger than the min(rt)?

The second question is: how can I check which model fits the data better. I thought about using wAIC (using this code <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/G9VuPvQchFY/CXPK9fV9BHoJ>). Is there an alternative/better way?
I'm extracting the log likelihood in this way:

    log_lik[i] <- normal_log(rt[i]-c[i],log_mu[i], sigma);

There's something wrong for sure, because I get a huge wAIC for the shifted lognormal, and the credible intervals are a bit wider than the ones of the lognormal distribution (even though I recover the mean of the parameters decently in both).

I'm posting the regular lmm, the shifted lognormal model, R code, and fake data that should have a  shifted lognormal distribution (betas =5, .12, .05,.08; shift = 180, sigma_shift = 60,sigma .7 )

Thanks!
Bruno

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling reaction time data with shifted log normal hierarchical model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Modeling reaction time data with shifted log normal hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for including the models.

You can ignore the Jacobian warning for subtract(rt,c) (corresponding
to model code "(rt - c) ~ ...".  Because c is a transformed parameter,
Stan can't track what might have happened to it at compile time (at least
in general, or in specific cases without a lot of work).
We should change wording of "contains a non-linear transform" to "may contain
a non-linear transform".

The other message is serious, because it's telling you that (rt - c) is
negative in some cases.  I have no idea what the [475] is doing there.  Daniel?
Given that rt[i] is data and c[i]  == (shift + shift_u[subj[i]]),
and shift is a scalar parameter, you need to constrain shift properly
to make sure

   shift < rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]]

for all i in 1:num_elements(rt).

functions {

  real shift_max(vector shift_u, int[] subj, vector rt) {
    real shift_max <- infinity();
    for (i in 1:num_elements(rt))
      shift_max <- min(shift_max, rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]]);
    return shift_max;
  }

}

You should most definitely check all my algebra here.  Then you
can declare:

  real<lower=0, upper=shift_max(shift_u,subj,rt)> shift;

Given that you're not averse to reading, I'd recommend the sections on
priors in the manual chapter on regression.  We've been advocating against
using this kind of thing

  real<lower=0,upper=10000> sigma;

in favor of unconstrained variables with at least weakly informative priors (e.g.,
if you expect sigma to be in the unit range, something like cauchy(0,5) or even
cauchy(0,2.5)).  The manual cites some papers by Andrew going over why the other
priors are bad news for inference.

As to fitting the data better, if you can afford the computation, and it
makes sense given your groupings, just use cross-validation.  You can build that
right in Stan.  I have it on my to-do list to add an example to the manual.

I think the issue you're going to have to deal with is marginalizing out all the latent
parameters if you want to properly compute a likelihood here.  But others are much
better than me at WAIC.  If the model comparison question gets buried in the noise
here, feel free to repost with a more directed title so those in the know (usually Andrew
or Aki, since they're most invested) see it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient implementation of average predictive comparison (APC, Gelman & Pardoe 2007)?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Efficient implementation of average predictive comparison (APC, Gelman & Pardoe 2007)?
messages.body_plain:
I'm going back through my old mail and realize we never answered
this one.  Sorry!  These huge questions often get put on the back
burner then never taken off until they start to burn.

I didn't understand all the moves in Gelman and Pardoe's approach,
so I don't have an opinion there.  For example, I don't see where
expectations come in given the definitions.

I'd have thought you could just write the model down and evaluate
y-hat(u) and y-hat(u + delta).  Or take a derivative using the
R interface (making sure to use unconstrained parameters to get it
on the model's scale).

- Bob

> On Jan 14, 2015, at 7:57 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I’d appreciate some feedback on the implementation of average predictive comparisons (APC; Gelman & Pardoe 2007) in stan (for now only for non-categorical variables).
>
>
> ######### if you know APC, jump over this section #######
>
> Background: In a nutshell, the APC provide an estimate about how much on average a response variable y changes for a one unit change in the predictor variable u, given all other predictor variables v are fixed.
>
>
>
>
>

> For example, one could examine the effect of the age, number of publications, number of citations,  on the response-variable “has tenure” by running a logistic regression. Calculating APCs for each variable would then  provide an estimate by how many percent the probability to be tenured increases for each age year, number of publications, number of publications, and number of citations, respectively.
>
>
> Equation 5 in Gelman & Pardoe (2007), describes an algorithm to estimate APCs and uses the following notation:
>
>
> 	• u, the variable of interest
>
> 	• v, a vector with the other variables
>
> 	• theta, the model parameters
>
> 	• yhat, the model prediction
>
> 	• n, the number data columns
>
> 	• S, the number of mcmc sample
>
>
> to estimate the APC for a variable u as
>
>
>

> here, E(yhat|u_j,v_i,theta_s) is a known function mapping data and parameters to predicted values (e.g. the inverse logit for logistic regressions). w_ij is a Mahalanobis-distance based weight that insuring comparisons u_i-u_j for which v_i and v_j are similar have a greater weight than comparisons u_i-u_j for which v_i and v_j are dissimilar. The term (u_j-u_i) in the denominator has the function to give smaller weight to comparisons with small differences of u, because these are potentially unstable due to noise or incomplete models. Finally, Gelman and Pardoe use the term sign(u_j-u_i) because their algorithm only considers cases where u_i<u_j. Otherwise the denominator and numerator would each sum to zero.
>
> ################### continue here ##################
>
>
>
> My APC implementation deviates a bit from a literal implementation of the equation above, and I’d like to know if if my implementation makes sense.
>
>
>
> In a nutshell, i prepare pairs for predictive comparisons and weights in the transformed parameters block calculate pair by pair predictive comparisons and their weighted average in the generated quantities block.
>
>
>
> (I) Generate pairs ui,uj for predictive comparisons
>
> Because I have too many data rows to make all pair comparisons in a reasonable amount of time, I submit 2 vectors u1s and u2s to stan, which contain row-numbers of the rows to be used to calculate the APCs. Pairs are created from indices in u1s and u2s by combining each u1 in u1s with each u2 in u2s. to avoid the problem of summation to zero, vectors u1s and u2s must be non-overlapping.
>
> In R for example i would create non-overlapping indices as follows:
>
> uidxs = sample(1:n,500,replace = F)  # sample 500 out of n rows
> u1s = uidxs[1:250]
> u2s = uidxs[251:500]
>
>
> For smaller data sets one could define all pairs in stan by looping only through the lower triangle of the matrix of all possible pairs u_i,u_j:
>
> for (u1 in 1:(n-1)) {
>  for (u2 in (u1+1):n){
>  ...
>  }
> }
>
>
> (II) Calculate weights in the transformed data block.
>
>
> I define weights as w_ij*|u_j-u_i|, where w_ij  is the  Mahalanobis distance based weight proposed by Gelman & Pardoe, and |u_j-u_i| downweights pairs with small differences in u.
>
> While this also follows Gelman and Pardoe, it still seems a bit ad hoc to me, because one could also omit this second term (when the model is complete and there is not to much noise) or one could take the sqrt(|ui-uj|) of it to avoid overweighting of extreme predictor values. (see also the discussion here: http://www.davidchudzicki.com/predcomps/more-pairs-and-weights.html)
>
>
>
>
> Because below I increment the APC comparison by comparison (i.e. I don’t first calculate separate sums for denominator and numerator), my weights have to sum to 1.
>
>
> stan code:
>
> (the full model code is attached)
>
>
> transformed data {
>   // matrix for weights
>   // K = number of predictor variables u (where the intercept is the first predictor)
>   // nus = number of indices first and second part of pair
>   matrix[K-1,nus*nus] weights;
>
>   // matrix for delta_u = u1-u2 to avoid calculating it repeatedly later
>   matrix[K-1,nus*nus] delta_u;
>
>   // matrices to store indices of nonzero u1-u2 differences
>   int<lower=0,upper=N> u1idx[K-1,nus*nus];
>   int<lower=0,upper=N> u2idx[K-1,nus*nus]
>
>   row_vector[K-2] delta_v;
>   matrix[1,1] mhlbd_sq;
>
>   // array to store number of nonzero differences u1-u2
>   int<lower=1> n_pairs[K-1];
>
>   n_pairs <- rep_array(0,K-1);
>   weights <- rep_matrix(0.0, K-1, nus*nus);
>
>
>   for (u in 2:K){ // loop through predictor variables
>     for (u1 in 1:nus){
>       for (u2 in 1:nus){
>         if (x[u1s[u1],u] != x[u2s[u2],u]) {
>           n_pairs[u-1] <- n_pairs[u-1]+1;
>
>           u1idx[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- u1s[u1];
>           u2idx[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- u2s[u2];
>
>           delta_u[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- x[u1s[u1],u] - x[u2s[u2],u];
>
>           // calculate vector delta_v  for Mahalanobis distance
>           // x is the design matrix for the regression, with the intercept in the first column
>          if( u == 2) {
>              delta_v <- sub_row(x,u1s[u1],u+1,K-u) - sub_row(x,u2s[u2],u+1,K-u);
>          } else if (u < K) {
>              delta_v <- append_col(sub_row(x,u1s[u1],2,u-2),sub_row(x,u1s[u1],u+1,K-u)) -
>                         append_col(sub_row(x,u2s[u2],2,u-2),sub_row(x,u2s[u2],u+1,K-u));
>          } else {
>              delta_v <- sub_row(x,u1s[u1],2,u-2) - sub_row(x,u2s[u2],2,u-2);
>          }
>
>
>          // square of mahalabonis distance between vectors v for u1 and u2
>          mhlbd_sq <- to_matrix(delta_v) * iCVs[u-1] * to_matrix(delta_v)';
>
>          // calculate weights from 2 parts: 1) |u1-u2|, 2) square of mahalabonis distance
>          weights[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- fabs(delta_u[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]])*1/(1+mhlbd_sq[1,1]);
>         }
>       }
>     }
>     // normalize weights so that they sum to 0
>     weights[u-1] <- weights[u-1]/sum(weights[u-1]);
>   }
>   print(n_pairs);
> }
>
> (III) Calculate APCs
>
>
> The basic idea to calculate the APC for a variable u is simple:
>
> 	• loop through all comparisons,
>
> 	• calculate a pair’s predictive comparison as (E(y|u_j,v_i,theta_s)-(E_y|u_i,v_i,theta_s))/(u_j-u_i)
>
> 	• multiply the pair's predictive comparison with its weight (which was prepared in the transformed parameters block)
>
> 	• increment the APC with the weighted predictive comparison
>
>
> stan code:
>
>
> generated quantities {
>   // array to store APCs
>   real APC[K-1];
>   APC <- rep_array(0,K-1);
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the fast answer! Unfortunately,  I got a long ugly error, see below:

On Saturday, March 14, 2015 at 1:32:22 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks for including the models.
>
> You can ignore the Jacobian warning for subtract(rt,c) (corresponding
> to model code "(rt - c) ~ ...".  Because c is a transformed parameter,
> Stan can't track what might have happened to it at compile time (at least
> in general, or in specific cases without a lot of work).
> We should change wording of "contains a non-linear transform" to "may contain
> a non-linear transform".
>
> The other message is serious, because it's telling you that (rt - c) is
> negative in some cases.  I have no idea what the [475] is doing there.  Daniel?
> Given that rt[i] is data and c[i]  == (shift + shift_u[subj[i]]),
> and shift is a scalar parameter, you need to constrain shift properly
> to make sure
>
>    shift < rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]]
>
> for all i in 1:num_elements(rt).
>
> functions {
>
>   real shift_max(vector shift_u, int[] subj, vector rt) {
>     real shift_max <- infinity();
>     for (i in 1:num_elements(rt))
>       shift_max <- min(shift_max, rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]]);
>     return shift_max;
>   }
>
> }

So I had  to change the function to:

functions {

  real shift_max(vector shift_u, int[] subj, vector rt) {

    real shift_max;
    real values[2];
    shift_max <- positive_infinity();
    for (i in 1:num_elements(rt)){
          values[1] <- shift_max;
          values[2] <- rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]];
          shift_max <- min(values);
        }
    return shift_max;
  }

}

in version 2.5 at least, min doesn't allow 2 reals, I don't know any more elegant way to initialize these two values. This  [shift_max,  rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]]] didn't work for me.
And I had to change infinity to positive _infinity and to put it in two lines. With this it started to compile but after a couple of seconds I got a very long error that I'm posting.

>
> You should most definitely check all my algebra here.  Then you
> can declare:
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=shift_max(shift_u,subj,rt)> shift;
>
> Given that you're not averse to reading, I'd recommend the sections on
> priors in the manual chapter on regression.  We've been advocating against
> using this kind of thing
>
>   real<lower=0,upper=10000> sigma;
>
> in favor of unconstrained variables with at least weakly informative priors (e.g.,
> if you expect sigma to be in the unit range, something like cauchy(0,5) or even
> cauchy(0,2.5)).  The manual cites some papers by Andrew going over why the other
> priors are bad news for inference.

Yes, since I was fitting different transformations of data in the other model, I was lazy to change the priors. But yes, I'm fixing that in shifted lognormal model.

>
> As to fitting the data better, if you can afford the computation, and it
> makes sense given your groupings, just use cross-validation.  You can build that
> right in Stan.  I have it on my to-do list to add an example to the manual.

Ok, I'll check that.

>
> I think the issue you're going to have to deal with is marginalizing out all the latent
> parameters if you want to properly compute a likelihood here.  But others are much
> better than me at WAIC.  If the model comparison question gets buried in the noise
> here, feel free to repost with a more directed title so those in the know (usually Andrew
> or Aki, since they're most invested) see it.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>
> > On Mar 14, 2015, at 1:29 AM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > I've been trying to fit some reading/reaction time (rt) data with a shifted log normal hierarchical model, where the shift also varies by subject. We (in psycholinguistics) usually use linear mixed models with lmer (from lme4 R package) and we either use log(rt) or (1/rt) as the dependent variable (to have it "normally distributed") and I would like to know if it's justified to fit a shifted-lognormal dist.
> >
> > So I built the model using Sorensen & Vasishth's tutorial and I followed Bob Carpenter's post for the log-shifted part . And I added shifts by subject.
> >

messages.body_plain:
I forgot our own function naming conventions, like positive_infinity().
fmax() and fmin() are the two-argument versions for reals (the "f" is
for floating point, which follows C++ convention and is hence confusing
in the Stan context).

We want to trap errors before they become compile-time errors and
spit out long ugly errors.  There's good news and bad news for this one.

The good news is that we know the source of the error and are working on a fix
for the next release, which we really hope to get out next week (but
no promises --- we're at least 50 person errors into fixing
this "upgrade" that included the nonstandard type __float128 and messed
up our autodiff, but we think we have it tackled).

The bad news is that you have to revert to an earlier compiler to fix it.
Or wait for the next release.  Or check out the current develop branch and
plug it in yourself (only easy with CmdStan).  Until our next release or until
you revert to an earlier compiler, I doubt any Stan program will compile.

- Bob

>   }
>

messages.subject: Am I using the 'fit' argument of the 'stan' function correctly?
messages.subject_clean: Am I using the 'fit' argument of the 'stan' function correctly?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I just wanted to check that I'm using the 'fit' argument of the 'stan' function (in Rstan) correctly. I am running a Monte Carlo simulation where some of my conditions that vary (such as number of items) affect how the model code is written and others (such as sample size) do not. This is probably due to my lack of familiarity of how to write good stan code, but that's the way it is right now. Do I need to compile one model fit object for every combination of conditions that vary (here, every combination of item length and sample size) regardless of whether they affect the stan model code, or can I save extra time by compiling one model fit object just for every combination of conditions that affect how the model code is written (here, every item length) and use that same fit object for different sample sizes with the same item length?

Thanks for the help,
Jon

If you write the Stan program to input things like n_length to the data block, then it should be fine. When stan() is passed a fit argument, it will pass whatever is in its data argument --- which can be different from when stan() was called originally --- to a new instance of the C++ object that does the sampling.

Ben

messages.subject: Stan 2.6.2 and CmdStan 2.6.2
messages.subject_clean: Stan 2.6.2 and CmdStan 2.6.2
messages.body_plain:
We've publicly released Stan and CmdStan versions 2.6.2.
As usual, check out the home page for download instructions:

  http://mc-stan.org/

BUG FIX RELEASE
---------------
This is a two-for-one special release because version 2.6.1
was never announced.  Only the patch version was incremented (from
2.6.0 to 2.6.2), indicating there are no new features in
this release and that it remains backward-compatible with
older releases.

NEW DEVELOPERS
--------------
We've added three new developers to the core dev team,
Brian Lau (MatlabStan), Rob Goedman (Stan.jl), and Jonah
Sol Gabry (ShinyStan).

CRAN
----
The main motivation was to fix some outstanding bugs and
allow compilation without the C++11 long long type and to fix
an issue with the non-standard __float128 type from g++ 4.9.
This was the last obstacle blocking RStan from being released
through CRAN.

BETTER PARSER ERROR MESSAGES
----------------------------
Although it didn't make it into the release notes, one thing you
may notice is that the parser for Stan programs should be returning
much more informative errors for syntactic errors in Stan programs.

OTHER BUG FIXES
---------------
Other outstanding issues fixed include properly rejecting
in normal CDFs when they hit a NaN arithmetically, which should
prevent Stan from terminating without samples in some situations.
We also fixed issue with append_row/_col return types, an
issue with indexing in the ODE solver, and an issue related
to double-indexing of matrices which caused errors to be raised
when values should have been returned.

The manual's also been updated to fix all the typos and brainos
we know of.

MAJOR REFACTORING OF MATH LIB
-----------------------------
There was also a huge amount of tidying up of directory and
include structure under the hood in the C++ API that is not
user facing, but should help us with longer-term maintenance.

Full release notes below, and we'll announce here again and
on Andrew's blog when RStan and PyStan have released 2.6.2.

- Stan Dev Team

v2.6.2 (14 March 2015)
======================================================================

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------------
* fixed append_row and append_col to return the corect types [#1297]
* documentation fix: fixed generation of stan-functions.txt [#1327]
* changed constructor of stan::agrad::var so it can compile without
  C++11 [#1337, 1364]
* fixed bug in matrix double-indexing [#1342]
* fixed calculation of derivative in normal_cdf_log, normal_ccdf_log
  [#1357]

API Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* refactored math / autodiff library [#1222, #1349, #1353]
* fixed capitalization in tests [#1355]
* updated Eigen to 3.2.4 [#1173]

v2.6.1 (3 March 2015)
======================================================================

Language Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* improved warning messages from the parser [#1244]

API/Build/Test Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* the C++ API now throws 3 types of exceptions [#685]
* parts of the C++ API were rearranged (gm, common) [#942]
* replace promote_args
* allow reading from a local makefile outside of the code repository [#1277]
* added gradient of hessian functional in C++ [#1272]
* supressed printing of adjoints when printing stan::agrad::var [#330]
* removed some cpplint warnings [#1282]
* removed doxygen warnings [#1290]
* reimplemented fmix and fmax [#1311]

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------------
* allow nested indexes to compile with integrate_ode [#1317]

Documentation
----------------------------------------
* fixed typos in MCMC sampling

Hi, I’m confused.  I just went to the Rstan installation page and it does not say anything about Cran.  So am I doing something wrong?
A

> On Mar 14, 2015, at 7:23 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> We've publicly released Stan and CmdStan versions 2.6.2.
> As usual, check out the home page for download instructions:
>
>  http://mc-stan.org/
>
>
> BUG FIX RELEASE
> ---------------
> This is a two-for-one special release because version 2.6.1
> was never announced.  Only the patch version was incremented (from
> 2.6.0 to 2.6.2), indicating there are no new features in
> this release and that it remains backward-compatible with
> older releases.
>
> NEW DEVELOPERS
> --------------
> We've added three new developers to the core dev team,
> Brian Lau (MatlabStan), Rob Goedman (Stan.jl), and Jonah
> Sol Gabry (ShinyStan).
>
> CRAN
> ----
> The main motivation was to fix some outstanding bugs and
> allow compilation without the C++11 long long type and to fix
> an issue with the non-standard __float128 type from g++ 4.9.
> This was the last obstacle blocking RStan from being released
> through CRAN.
>
> BETTER PARSER ERROR MESSAGES
> ----------------------------
> Although it didn't make it into the release notes, one thing you
> may notice is that the parser for Stan programs should be returning
> much more informative errors for syntactic errors in Stan programs.
>
> OTHER BUG FIXES
> ---------------
> Other outstanding issues fixed include properly rejecting
> in normal CDFs when they hit a NaN arithmetically, which should
> prevent Stan from terminating without samples in some situations.
> We also fixed issue with append_row/_col return types, an
> issue with indexing in the ODE solver, and an issue related
> to double-indexing of matrices which caused errors to be raised
> when values should have been returned.
>
> The manual's also been updated to fix all the typos and brainos
> we know of.
>
> MAJOR REFACTORING OF MATH LIB
> -----------------------------
> There was also a huge amount of tidying up of directory and
> include structure under the hood in the C++ API that is not
> user facing, but should help us with longer-term maintenance.
>
> Full release notes below, and we'll announce here again and
> on Andrew's blog when RStan and PyStan have released 2.6.2.
>
> - Stan Dev Team
>
>
> v2.6.2 (14 March 2015)
> ======================================================================
>
> Bug Fixes
> ----------------------------------------
> * fixed append_row and append_col to return the corect types [#1297]
> * documentation fix: fixed generation of stan-functions.txt [#1327]
> * changed constructor of stan::agrad::var so it can compile without
>  C++11 [#1337, 1364]
> * fixed bug in matrix double-indexing [#1342]
> * fixed calculation of derivative in normal_cdf_log, normal_ccdf_log
>  [#1357]
>
> API Enhancements
> ----------------------------------------
> * refactored math / autodiff library [#1222, #1349, #1353]
> * fixed capitalization in tests [#1355]
> * updated Eigen to 3.2.4 [#1173]
>
>
>
> v2.6.1 (3 March 2015)
> ======================================================================
>
> Language Enhancements
> ----------------------------------------
> * improved warning messages from the parser [#1244]
>
> API/Build/Test Enhancements
> ----------------------------------------
> * the C++ API now throws 3 types of exceptions [#685]
> * parts of the C++ API were rearranged (gm, common) [#942]
> * replace promote_args
> * allow reading from a local makefile outside of the code repository [#1277]
> * added gradient of hessian functional in C++ [#1272]
> * supressed printing of adjoints when printing stan::agrad::var [#330]
> * removed some cpplint warnings [#1282]
> * removed doxygen warnings [#1290]
> * reimplemented fmix and fmax [#1311]
>
> Bug Fixes
> ----------------------------------------
> * allow nested indexes to compile with integrate_ode [#1317]
>
> Documentation
> ----------------------------------------
> * fixed typos in MCMC sampling
>
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure how you could then code the rest of the model,
but it's not a good idea in Stan because your d2 will not
be sampled well because there is no gradient information (it
gets lost in the transform to d).

To build this in Stan, you want to create a mixture model of lags
1 to 10, then build up an array lp[10] where lp[d] is the
log density of the component for lag d.  Then use

   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));

There's a chapter in the manual on mixture models and another
on marginalizing discrete parameters that you may find helpful in
doing this.

The choice I see you facing is whether to tie the parameters
at lag d across d, d + 1, ..., 10 so that they're the same
for all mixture components.  I would guess you would want
separate parameters, because that's closest to the model comparison
approach.

What we generally recommend in these situations is to just fit
the d == 10 case with priors on the lag components that will
shrink the effects toward zero if there is not enough data to
support them.  It will be much more efficient (10 vs. 10^2 work
and probably an easier model to fit), and you can then just inspect
the parameters to see if there are effects at longer lags.

- Bob

Sometimes I forget the basics, especially when working in these higher-level frameworks. This is very close to what we are trying to infer.   Pr[n in same cluster as n’, n’’, … | y]

can this be calculated downstream from the Pr[n in same cluster as n’| y]? Calculating it for all given combinations seems unfeasible.

Of course, this does not capture the generative process exactly, as each of the places are physically connected sequentially (i.e. 1-2-3-4-5, …). But practically, that might be OK. If each of the clusters represent a physical complex (a set of proteins), and assuming each protein can be a member of multiple clusters, 1,000 is not an unreasonable high number.

mixture component.  If you want to relax this, you need to go to
some kind of mixed-membership model like LDA.

Yes, anything combinatoric like this is intractable.

do.  People often try to fudge this with something like k-means
or LDA, but those are so highly multimodal in their posteriors,
you can't actually do the proper inference.  Every initial point
leads to a different local maximum and different inferences.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
messages.body_plain:
No, HMC won't work if there's no gradient information.  There's no
guarantee you'll get the right distribution in the end if the
function's not differentiable on its support.

It'll work the same way whether you build the mixture as 1 to 10
or 1 to T/10 (don't do /10.0, or you'll get a floating point
number --- T/10 will round down).

But as I said before, I'd try just building one time series and
inspecting the parameters to judge how long-distance the effects
are.

- Bob

On Mar 17, 2015, at 1:44 AM, He-chien Tsai <depo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The model's maximum lag-order is not 10 and is depends on length of time series (T / 10.0). I originally use metaheuristic algorithm with WAIC as target function to determine lag-order, mixturing all models may exhausts computing power and memory.
> keeping all lag components doesn't fit my need because some integer parameters are breaking point of time series.
> I'm not familiar how NUTS sampler works but I think sampling may eliminates the use of metaheuristic algorithm.
> Can NUTS sampler work even there is no gradient information? How bad would it be?
>
> On Monday, March 16, 2015 at 7:15:24 AM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm not sure how you could then code the rest of the model,
> but it's not a good idea in Stan because your d2 will not
> be sampled well because there is no gradient information (it
> gets lost in the transform to d).
>
> To build this in Stan, you want to create a mixture model of lags
> 1 to 10, then build up an array lp[10] where lp[d] is the
> log density of the component for lag d.  Then use
>
>    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
>
> There's a chapter in the manual on mixture models and another
> on marginalizing discrete parameters that you may find helpful in
> doing this.
>
> The choice I see you facing is whether to tie the parameters
> at lag d across d, d + 1, ..., 10 so that they're the same
> for all mixture components.  I would guess you would want
> separate parameters, because that's closest to the model comparison
> approach.
>
> What we generally recommend in these situations is to just fit
> the d == 10 case with priors on the lag components that will
> shrink the effects toward zero if there is not enough data to
> support them.  It will be much more efficient (10 vs. 10^2 work
> and probably an easier model to fit), and you can then just inspect
> the parameters to see if there are effects at longer lags.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: cholesky_factor_corr and standard deviations to cholesky_factor_cov?
messages.subject_clean: cholesky_factor_corr and standard deviations to cholesky_factor_cov?
messages.body_plain:
I am back trying to adjust myself to Stan syntax.  As I understand the approach to incorporating the covariance matrix, say as the covariance of vector-valued random effects in a mixed-effects model, the distribution is defined on the correlation matrix but it is the choleksy factor of the covariance matrix that is used in multi_normal_cholesky.

I seem to be confused about what a cholesky_factor_corr is and whether it can be used as a matrix in a multiplication or in multi_normal_cholesky.

Suppose I have a very simple case like

parameters {
  cholesky_factor_corr[J] L;    // Cholesky factor of unconditional correlation of random effects
#  vector[J]  tau;                // Unconditional standard deviations of the random effects
  vector[J] b[N]; // random effects on original scale
  vector[K] beta; // fixed-effects
  real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation of response given random effects
}

model {
#  tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  for (j in 1:J)
    b[j] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(0,L);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(dot(Xt[n],beta) + dot(Zt[n],b[subj[n]]),sigma);
}

This fails to compile, apparently because L is not a matrix.

SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="multi_normal_cholesky_log"
    arg 0 type=vector
    arg 1 type=int
    arg 2 type=matrix
available function signatures for multi_normal_cholesky_log:
0.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector, vector, matrix) : real
1.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector, row vector, matrix) : real
2.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector, vector, matrix) : real
3.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector, row vector, matrix) : real
4.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector, vector[1], matrix) : real
5.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector, row vector[1], matrix) : real
6.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector, vector[1], matrix) : real
7.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector, row vector[1], matrix) : real
8.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector[1], vector, matrix) : real
9.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector[1], row vector, matrix) : real
10.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector[1], vector, matrix) : real
11.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector[1], row vector, matrix) : real
12.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector[1], vector[1], matrix) : real
13.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(vector[1], row vector[1], matrix) : real
14.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector[1], vector[1], matrix) : real
15.  multi_normal_cholesky_log(row vector[1], row vector[1], matrix) : real

Do I need to do something to make L act like a matrix?

Once I get past this I want to incorporate tau in the model.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] cholesky_factor_corr and standard deviations to cholesky_factor_cov?
messages.body_plain:
That error message is saying that multi_normal_log can't be called with the signature vector, integer, matrix. It's because you're using:

b[j] ~ multi_normal_log(0, L)

When you should be using:

 b[j] ~ multi_normal_log(rep_vector(0, J), L)

multi_normal_log needs the dimensionally of the first two arguments to match (as well as the type).

cholesky_factor_corr can indeed be used in multiplications, but if you want to use it for multi_normal_log, you'll need to use code in the transformed parameters block to turn it into a proper covariance matrix by multiplying by a vector of standard deviations 2X.

Rob

Apologies on that last piece of advice, it was wrong. Just add the block:

transformed parameters {
cholesky_factor_cov[J] chol_mat;

chol_mat <- diag_pre_multily(tau, L)
}

And change your tau line to read:

vector<lower=0> tau;

And your multi_normal_log line to:

b[j] ~ multi_normal_log(rep_vector(0,J), chol_mat)

The best advice for putting a multivariate normal prior on your beta's will be on page 63 of the manual. Following that code will allow you to do away with your multi_normal_log statement.

Rob

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 18, 2015, at 8:10 AM, Robert Trangucci <robert.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Apologies on that last piece of advice, it was wrong. Just add the block:
>
> transformed parameters {
> cholesky_factor_cov[J] chol_mat;
>
> chol_mat <- diag_pre_multily(tau, L)
> }
>

I would strongly suggest using cholesky_factor_corr here
and an LKJ prior which is like the beta but for correlation
matrices --- as the dof parameter goes up, it concentrates
mass around the unit matrix.

It's just a more interpretable way of doing what Andrew and
Jennifer were suggesting in their regression book.

Ben has a very nice paper on the LKJ vs. Wisharts:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

> And change your tau line to read:
>
> vector<lower=0> tau;
>
> And your multi_normal_log line to:
>
> b[j] ~ multi_normal_log(rep_vector(0,J), chol_mat)

I'd also suggest defining rep_vector(0,J) in the transformed
data block so it's only allocated and filled once.

Then doesn't this have to be multi_normal_cholesky(...).
What you have won't work, as it needs to be multi_normal(), not
multi_normal_log --- the former is the sampling statement syntax,
the latter the function name.

> The best advice for putting a multivariate normal prior on your beta's will be on page 63 of the manual. Following that code will allow you to do away with your multi_normal_log statement.

Agreed.

- Bob

On Wednesday, March 18, 2015 at 2:23:42 PM UTC-4, Douglas Bates wrote:
> I still would appreciate learning if there is a way to access a matrix column as a vector.

Probably

col(X, k)

is what you need to extract the k-th column of X. But it can be more efficient to represent a NxK "matrix" as a K-array of N-vectors

vector[N] X[K];

in which case you could just access the k-th "column" with X[k]. Bob has been working on some R-like syntax --- such as X[1:N,k] --- but it is not merged yet.

Ben

messages.subject: Performance penalty using truncated priors?
messages.subject_clean: Performance penalty using truncated priors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am working with additive models where I frequently need to constrain the sign of the fitting coefficient, e.g.

y = a * x1 + b * x2 + c * x3

say I want a to be positive and have a decreasing prior for large values. I typically do this using one of these priors

a ~ normal(0, 50) T[0.0,];

or

a ~ gamma(1, 0.025);

where I define

real<lower=0> a;

in both cases.

My question is whether I suffer in performance, using the truncated normal distribution compared to the inherently positive gamma distribution?

Thanks in advance,
Per

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Performance penalty using truncated priors?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Performance penalty using truncated priors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Per,

I'll start by answering your question:
  No, you will not suffer in computational performance by using the
truncated normal distribution, or any other distribution.

If you declare `a` as a parameter:
   real<lower=0> a;

Truncating the prior is computationally worse. Instead of

   a ~ normal(0, 50) T[0.0,];

use
   a ~ normal(0, 50);

The additive model might really suffer with such wide priors if the
data don't provide much information.

Question: have you tried both the normal and gamma? The nice thing
about Stan is that you can actually build both models and try them out
on your data.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: fitting multiple sets of data with same model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: fitting multiple sets of data with same model
messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 20, 2015, at 1:19 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 2:16:51 AM UTC-4, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
> hi guys,
>
> Many thanks.
>
> Yes, my original question was more about parallel development as I'm trying to get my arms around development with STAN/rstan in terms of how to split the codes across the 2 layers.
>
> Do as much outside of Stan itself as possible---the reason is you'll need it in R anyway for flexible model checking anyway and while Stan is quite flexible in its transformed data block
> it's not as easy to trouble shoot as R (though amazing compared to BUGS).  If you do anything in the parameters/transformed parameter/model block that could be instead done in R (or the
> transformed data block) you're wasting CPU time as it gets done once per leapfrog step (many times per iteration).

The number of times the transformed parameters and model blocks
get executed is upper bounded by 2^(treedepth + 1), but it's usually
exactly 2^treedepth.  CmdStan actually dumps out the number of leapfrog
steps now, I believe.

But the real killer is that any variables introduced in the model
block or transformed parameters block go on the autodiff stack,
which makes taking gradients slower, and that's the real bottleneck.

Anything that can be moved from transformed parameters to either

  * transformed data:  operates on doubles, once per chain

  * generated quantities:  operates on doubles, once per iteration

is a big win.  I'm guessing using our generated quantities would
save CPU time vs. R, but the problem is that it gets written into the
output file, which sucks up memory if you're running through R or
I/O if you run through CmdStan.

- Bob
