messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Thank you for building such a great tool. I’ve been using rstan with great success over the past year, and until now have been able to sort out my problems on my own. However, I’m now having an issue with something that seems simple, but I can’t figure out what’s going on.

The model is a hierarchical probit model, with simulated data of individuals purchasing a given product. Individuals are simulated to have 20 observations each, where the person either buys or does not buy at each occassion, and the covariates are the price and an indicator for coupon, all set randomly. The simulation is included in the attached code.

I am having problems with the initialization: regardless of whether I set the inits, or let stan do it, I get the same error:

“SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'probit' NOW (CHAIN 1).
Error :

Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done”

I have tried initializing at exactly the simulated values and get the error. There are a few other things I’ve investigated.
The non-hierarchical equivalent has no issues, with the parameter set at the prior mean from the hierarchical version
The same error presents regardless of the hyperprior specification. I have tried not specifying a hyper prior, set it to be Wishart, Inverse Wishart, and as you can see in the attached, the recommended LKJ formulation from the stan reference manual. Regardless, I get this error.
I have tried specifying the model in a vectorized form (beta and y vectorized), and nothing changes.
I’ve tried varying the simulation parameters and the initialization, and nothing changes the error.

I believe I’ve set the constraints correctly, and I don’t think there is anything noteworthy (bad or good) about the parametrization, but undoubtedly I'm wrong on one of these. Please let me know if you have any insight!

Thanks for your help!

Ryan

messages.body_plain:
I don't see any immediate problem with the constraints.
How big is K?  There may be instability with the correlation
matrix or multiplication.

In general, you're better off using a Cholesky factor
parameterization instead of a full-on covariance matrix.

There's an example in the manual, but the basic idea is
that you are much better for for arithmetic stability and
efficiency with:

  cholesky_corr[K] L_Omega;
...

  matrix[K,K] L_Sigma;
  L_Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega);

  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);

You can then reconstruct Omega as L_Omega * L_Omega'
in the generated quantities if you want to look at it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I also want to add that I discovered far too late that, after my initial trials with inits and no inits, I had forgotten to re-include the init part of the stan() command, as evident in the code I posted at the start. So for some of my initial value trials, it wasn't actually calling the specified inits. When I legitimately initialize the posted model at the true parameter values, it does work, and also at random values near zero, although the cholesky factorization version is much more stable (at a wide range of starting values) and more efficient. I discovered this only after I had the cholesky version up and running, and it's a pretty embarrassing mistake, but since I've referenced more than a handful of these threads looking for solutions to problems, I wanted to include this endnote in case anyone else has this problem.

Thanks again for the help.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow convergence of high-dimensional gaussian process model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your comments; any help is very much appreciated : )

About the covariance function; it is a special case of the one recommended in the Stan manual. That covariance function has three parameters: sigma_sq, eta_sq and rho_sq. Sigma_sq is not needed for logistic regression. Eta_sq is a constant that multiplies the entire matrix; by omitting it in the model, I have effectively set it to 1. The modeling logic behind this is that, in the case where there is only one game, the priors on the team coefficients should be i.i.d. N(0,1).

Now, you say that something that constrains team performance over time is necessary. But that something is already in the model; it is rho_sq! Rho_sq can be made arbitrarily small in order to make the performance over time highly correlated, and it is the case that the coefficients are already very highly correlated. The tests I have been running have been tried with only two observations for each team, a week apart, and the observations have a correlation of exp(-0.15*0.04) = 0.994. In other words, the performance is very constrained over time. That is actually the problem! Separability is definitely not an issue here; I can make all the correlations zero and get a diagonal covariance matrix and the sampler runs just fine.

Now that brings the question of why on earth I am modeling it as time-varying only to have the parameters barely change. There are two answers. One, the correlation over a couple months, or years, would certainly be much smaller, but still significant. Two, even if a team's ability today is 90% correlated with its ability in a few months, the variation is important in order to predict game outcomes. Modeling it as fixed in time can lead to drastically different result predictions.

Why am I not estimating rho_sq and cuts and doing full bayesian inference? Well, I haven't even managed to do inference with a subset of the parameters, so I am certainly not going to try and do it with all three! Maybe if I get this sampler to run faster I can try moving rho_sq and cuts to the parameter block, but for now this seems like it would just complicate things more. The values I use are just "ultra informative priors" I estimated in other ways; for cuts, by sampling from a time-fixed model, and for rho_sq, by optimizing a model where the values are correlated across seasons, but fixed within each season.

I might try working with the time series model. I went with the GP model because it is more intuitive, more elegant, and more accurate, but of course all of that is no good if it can't be fit in less than a day. I agree that it  should probably run much faster than the GP model.

Since I started this discussion, I have played around with max_treedepth using tidbits of information from old threads on the list. I found out that increasing max_treedepth significantly improves my ESS/iteration ratio. A tree depth of 15 brought me to 10%. However, it also makes the running time significantly longer; the overall effect on ESS/time is a wash. I will try using smaller step sizes and/or larger acceptance rates then; hopefully I can make some headway with one of those. I don't think initialization will make a significant difference; the sampler has no problem getting estimates that are in the correct range of values very quickly. I can post some traceplots; maybe that will help with diagnosing the pathology.

Thanks for all the help! And if I may, can I ask about the RStan optimization problem? There is no way it can be due to a lack of a posterior mode, so what other possibility is there? Any ideas? I believe that getting the point estimates from the model may be the ideal path for me, since full bayesian inference is likely to take ages to be done.

I think one problem here is numerical stability. Sigma is "almost" singular (reciprocal condition number about 1e-10). Adding small amount of jitter to diagonal terms of Sigma should help a bit. Also, maybe increase the value of rho_sq? (current value implies correlation almost 1 for each team&time and is big part of these problems). If at some point you want to estimate rho_sq (or other covariance function parameters), then I think a better idea would be to use multiple team specific covariance matrices instead of putting them all together. As far as I can see, it would give exactly the same results and avoids inverting much larger matrix while sampling.

Anyway, I think Bob's suggestion about using simple time series models is a good one. I do remember reading an article using exactly that kind of model for football predictions (found a link: https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/dspace-jspui/bitstream/2134/8929/3/owen_extended_paper_REVISED_29th_Nov_2010_CHANGES_ACCEPTED%5B1%5D.pdf )

messages.subject_clean: Approximate mcmc samples using a smaller subset
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

Is it possible to create a smaller set of mcmc samples, which approximately maintains the properties of the original joint posterior/mcmc samples? The most important properties to maintain are the MAP position and linear pairwise correlations between parameters.

I am interested in this as point estimates for my parameters (MAP, mean, median), do not reproduce the mean predictions of my models very well, and running the model on all the original mcmc samples is infeasible for my applications.

Thanks,
Per

messages.body_plain:
That is a slightly different but ultimately similar problem.

Formally MCMC generates samples to construct MCMC
estimators of expectations — the more samples the more
precise those estimators.  Given sufficient regularity
conditions the precision for an estimate is given by the
(Markov chain) Monte Carlo central limit theorem,

MCSE( E[f] ) = Var[f] / ESS

where Var[f] is the true variance of the function f and
ESS is the effective sample size which summarizes
the autocorrelations of your chain.  Var[f] is typically
estimated with MCMC itself (Stan does this
automatically), while ESS is estimated with using
an FFT-based autocorrelation estimator.

Anyways, the point is that you have to first define
what level of precision you need in your application
and then compute the variance of each estimator.
That defines the ESS you need.  If your posteriors
samples have a much larger ESS then you can thin
them (removing samples at equal intervals) until you
hit your ESS threshold, but that’s it.  If you need
serious precision then you’ll need all your samples.

messages.body_plain:
You won't be able to recover the posterior mode (MAP
estimate) from a sample (set of draws from the posterior).
It's especially tricky in higher dimensions --- for a high
dimensional Gaussian, most of the posterior mass is not near
the posterior mode.

But if the joint posterior mode exists, you can run Stan's
optimizer to find it --- it's a much easier problem than
estimating the posterior mean computationally.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for following up here Bob!
I ended up implementing the APC calculation as described in Gelman and Pardoe.
My main problem was not implementing the algorithm, but the fact that for larger
data sets it becomes prohibitively expensive to calculate APCs for the  full data.
Similar to what David has done in his predcomps package, I am now calculating APCs on subsamples
of the data (I am still fitting the full data set). because APCs are calculated for each sample I
then examine convergence of APCs from chains that calculate APCs for different subsets of the data.

I am attaching the code for the model. (I am warning ahead that it is messy, and that most lines of code
are used to scale the data and set up the calculation of APCs in the transformed data block)

Guido

On Saturday, March 14, 2015 at 5:32:22 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm going back through my old mail and realize we never answered
> this one.  Sorry!  These huge questions often get put on the back
> burner then never taken off until they start to burn.
>
> I didn't understand all the moves in Gelman and Pardoe's approach,
> so I don't have an opinion there.  For example, I don't see where
> expectations come in given the definitions.
>
> I'd have thought you could just write the model down and evaluate
> y-hat(u) and y-hat(u + delta).  Or take a derivative using the
> R interface (making sure to use unconstrained parameters to get it
> on the model's scale).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Jan 14, 2015, at 7:57 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I’d appreciate some feedback on the implementation of average predictive comparisons (APC; Gelman & Pardoe 2007) in stan (for now only for non-categorical variables).
> >
> >
> > ######### if you know APC, jump over this section #######
> >
> > Background: In a nutshell, the APC provide an estimate about how much on average a response variable y changes for a one unit change in the predictor variable u, given all other predictor variables v are fixed.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > For example, one could examine the effect of the age, number of publications, number of citations,  on the response-variable “has tenure” by running a logistic regression. Calculating APCs for each variable would then  provide an estimate by how many percent the probability to be tenured increases for each age year, number of publications, number of publications, and number of citations, respectively.
> >
> >
> > Equation 5 in Gelman & Pardoe (2007), describes an algorithm to estimate APCs and uses the following notation:
> >
> >
> >         • u, the variable of interest
> >
> >         • v, a vector with the other variables
> >
> >         • theta, the model parameters
> >
> >         • yhat, the model prediction
> >
> >         • n, the number data columns
> >
> >         • S, the number of mcmc sample
> >
> >
> > to estimate the APC for a variable u as
> >
> >
> >
> > here, E(yhat|u_j,v_i,theta_s) is a known function mapping data and parameters to predicted values (e.g. the inverse logit for logistic regressions). w_ij is a Mahalanobis-distance based weight that insuring comparisons u_i-u_j for which v_i and v_j are similar have a greater weight than comparisons u_i-u_j for which v_i and v_j are dissimilar. The term (u_j-u_i) in the denominator has the function to give smaller weight to comparisons with small differences of u, because these are potentially unstable due to noise or incomplete models. Finally, Gelman and Pardoe use the term sign(u_j-u_i) because their algorithm only considers cases where u_i<u_j. Otherwise the denominator and numerator would each sum to zero.
> >
> > ################### continue here ##################
> >
> >
> >
> > My APC implementation deviates a bit from a literal implementation of the equation above, and I’d like to know if if my implementation makes sense.
> >
> >
> >
> > In a nutshell, i prepare pairs for predictive comparisons and weights in the transformed parameters block calculate pair by pair predictive comparisons and their weighted average in the generated quantities block.
> >
> >
> >
> > (I) Generate pairs ui,uj for predictive comparisons
> >
> > Because I have too many data rows to make all pair comparisons in a reasonable amount of time, I submit 2 vectors u1s and u2s to stan, which contain row-numbers of the rows to be used to calculate the APCs. Pairs are created from indices in u1s and u2s by combining each u1 in u1s with each u2 in u2s. to avoid the problem of summation to zero, vectors u1s and u2s must be non-overlapping.
> >
> > In R for example i would create non-overlapping indices as follows:
> >
> > uidxs = sample(1:n,500,replace = F)  # sample 500 out of n rows
> > u1s = uidxs[1:250]
> > u2s = uidxs[251:500]
> >
> >
> > For smaller data sets one could define all pairs in stan by looping only through the lower triangle of the matrix of all possible pairs u_i,u_j:
> >
> > for (u1 in 1:(n-1)) {
> >  for (u2 in (u1+1):n){
> >  ...
> >  }
> > }
> >
> >
> > (II) Calculate weights in the transformed data block.
> >
> >
> > I define weights as w_ij*|u_j-u_i|, where w_ij  is the  Mahalanobis distance based weight proposed by Gelman & Pardoe, and |u_j-u_i| downweights pairs with small differences in u.
> >
> > While this also follows Gelman and Pardoe, it still seems a bit ad hoc to me, because one could also omit this second term (when the model is complete and there is not to much noise) or one could take the sqrt(|ui-uj|) of it to avoid overweighting of extreme predictor values. (see also the discussion here: http://www.davidchudzicki.com/predcomps/more-pairs-and-weights.html)
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Because below I increment the APC comparison by comparison (i.e. I don’t first calculate separate sums for denominator and numerator), my weights have to sum to 1.
> >
> >
> > stan code:
> >
> > (the full model code is attached)
> >
> >
> > transformed data {
> >   // matrix for weights
> >   // K = number of predictor variables u (where the intercept is the first predictor)
> >   // nus = number of indices first and second part of pair
> >   matrix[K-1,nus*nus] weights;
> >
> >   // matrix for delta_u = u1-u2 to avoid calculating it repeatedly later
> >   matrix[K-1,nus*nus] delta_u;
> >
> >   // matrices to store indices of nonzero u1-u2 differences
> >   int<lower=0,upper=N> u1idx[K-1,nus*nus];
> >   int<lower=0,upper=N> u2idx[K-1,nus*nus]
> >
> >   row_vector[K-2] delta_v;
> >   matrix[1,1] mhlbd_sq;
> >
> >   // array to store number of nonzero differences u1-u2
> >   int<lower=1> n_pairs[K-1];
> >
> >   n_pairs <- rep_array(0,K-1);
> >   weights <- rep_matrix(0.0, K-1, nus*nus);
> >
> >
> >   for (u in 2:K){ // loop through predictor variables
> >     for (u1 in 1:nus){
> >       for (u2 in 1:nus){
> >         if (x[u1s[u1],u] != x[u2s[u2],u]) {
> >           n_pairs[u-1] <- n_pairs[u-1]+1;
> >
> >           u1idx[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- u1s[u1];
> >           u2idx[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- u2s[u2];
> >
> >           delta_u[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- x[u1s[u1],u] - x[u2s[u2],u];
> >
> >           // calculate vector delta_v  for Mahalanobis distance
> >           // x is the design matrix for the regression, with the intercept in the first column
> >          if( u == 2) {
> >              delta_v <- sub_row(x,u1s[u1],u+1,K-u) - sub_row(x,u2s[u2],u+1,K-u);
> >          } else if (u < K) {
> >              delta_v <- append_col(sub_row(x,u1s[u1],2,u-2),sub_row(x,u1s[u1],u+1,K-u)) -
> >                         append_col(sub_row(x,u2s[u2],2,u-2),sub_row(x,u2s[u2],u+1,K-u));
> >          } else {
> >              delta_v <- sub_row(x,u1s[u1],2,u-2) - sub_row(x,u2s[u2],2,u-2);
> >          }
> >
> >
> >          // square of mahalabonis distance between vectors v for u1 and u2
> >          mhlbd_sq <- to_matrix(delta_v) * iCVs[u-1] * to_matrix(delta_v)';
> >
> >          // calculate weights from 2 parts: 1) |u1-u2|, 2) square of mahalabonis distance
> >          weights[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- fabs(delta_u[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]])*1/(1+mhlbd_sq[1,1]);
> >         }
> >       }
> >     }
> >     // normalize weights so that they sum to 0
> >     weights[u-1] <- weights[u-1]/sum(weights[u-1]);
> >   }
> >   print(n_pairs);
> > }
> >
> > (III) Calculate APCs
> >
> >
> > The basic idea to calculate the APC for a variable u is simple:
> >
> >         • loop through all comparisons,
> >
> >         • calculate a pair’s predictive comparison as (E(y|u_j,v_i,theta_s)-(E_y|u_i,v_i,theta_s))/(u_j-u_i)
> >
> >         • multiply the pair's predictive comparison with its weight (which was prepared in the transformed parameters block)
> >
> >         • increment the APC with the weighted predictive comparison
> >
> >
> > stan code:
> >
> >
> > generated quantities {
> >   // array to store APCs
> >   real APC[K-1];
> >   APC <- rep_array(0,K-1);
> >
> >   for (u in 2:K){ // loop through predictor variables
> >     for (k in 1:n_pairs[u-1]) { // loop through pairs with nonzero difference u1-u2
> >       // increment            eta=log(mu) of a neg. binomial  * weight
> >       APC[u-1] <- APC[u-1] + (exp(eta[u1idx[u-1,k]])-exp(eta[u2idx[u-1,k]]))/delta_u[u-1,k] * weights[u-1,k];
> >     }
> >   }
> > }
> >
> >
> >
> > Finally, I am uncertain about the use of matrices vs arrays. I could glean from the stan-reference that arrays have the advantage that values can be returned by reference. On the other hand, I also read that "traversing matrices is more efficient than traversing arrays" (though I haven't checked yet if I am traversing them in the right order). I am not sure what is more relevant here.
> >
> > Speed is certainly an issue, because with the current code the sampling phase is slower than the warmup phase.
> >
> >
> > Best - Guido
> >
> >
> >

CmdStan writes out every iteration to disk, so it already does what you're asking for. If you thin, it'll only write the iterations you ask to save, but it'll do it after the iteration is done.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I’m stuck on something.  In some ways it’s no big deal cos I could do it in R, but I’d like to stay within Stan if possible.

It’s a question about generated quantities, and it comes from the project with Sebastian and Amy on the incorporation of aggregate data into a Bayesian analysis.

Currently I have a Stan program (attached in this message) that I wrote.  The program works as follows:

- In the model block, I compute the log posterior given the data matrix y.

- In the generated quantities block, I first simulate an external parameter delta (from a prior distribution input into the Stan model) and then I simulate a fake data matrix y_tilde.  For each posterior simulation draw (i.e., in each call to the generated quantities block), I simulate 100 fake data matrices and then compute their covariance matrix, then from there I compute an importance weight which is used in later calculations.

What I’ve been doing is iterating:  I start with a guess of the prior for the external parameter delta, then I run the Stan program, then I use the results to come up with a new prior, then I re-run the Stan program, etc.

But, what I realized is, I shouldn’t really need to be re-fitting the model each time.  Really all I should need to do is to re-run the generated quantities block with the updated prior but with the same posterior simulations of the parameters from the model block.

So, here’s my question:  Can we call Stan using existing posterior simulations?  I think the answer is No, so that I’ll just have to do my generating in R.  Which I can do, it just seems too bad that I can’t do it all in Stan.

Any help would be appreciated.  It’s not urgent but it’s buggin me.  Thanks.

A

messages.body_plain:
I think the best way to do this is to user-define a Stan function that ends in _rng

matrix foo_rng(matrix input) {
  // do random-number generation
  // return whatever
}

export that function to R (only rstan 2.6.3 is capable of doing this at the moment), and then call that function from R.

E.g. I did this to calculate the WAIC from R

# WAIC implied by normal log-likelihood
vector WAIC(vector y, matrix X, /* N rows */
            vector intercept, matrix beta,
           /* parameters all have S draws */
           vector sigma) {

  vector[2] out; out <- rep_vector(0,2);
  for(i in 1:rows(X)) {
    vector[rows(beta)] ll;
    vector[rows(beta)] mu; mu <- intercept +
     beta * transpose(row(X,i));
    for(j in 1:rows(beta)) ll[j] <-
      normal_log(y[i], mu[j], sigma[j]);
    out[1] <- out[1] + log(mean(exp(ll)));
    out[2] <- out[2] + variance(ll);
  }
  out[1] <- -2 * (out[1] - out[2]);
  return out; # out[1] is WAIC, out[2] is p_WAIC
}

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure what your model is.  The first thing to do
is write the model down in math.  Then if it has discrete
parameters, marginalize them out.

None of that depends on Stan.

When you have that, we can help you translate to Stan.
As is, I don't understand your model well enough to help
and trying to infer it from a broken Stan program isn't
so easy.

I can tell you that the problem in your multiplication is
that you can only multiply vectors, not arrays. There's a
chapter in the manual on arrays vs. vectors you might find
useful in this regard.

- Bob

> On Mar 28, 2015, at 8:16 AM, Sierra <sierra.ch...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

>

>
> As you can see from my original code, I am quite confused about summing out over classes K while incrementing the log probability, etc. A part of my confusion is what to sum over because the model is hierarchical but not everything varies over classes... and I am new around here.
>
> Only the vector on the means varies over classes.... is that the only portion where I need to sum over classes? The core model is simply something like:
>     eta[n]~MVN[3](mu_eta[k],Sigma_eta)
>     y[n]~N(X*eta,sigma_y)
>
> Right now my code isn't working at all (ill-formed expression for the multiplication in the normal log.... I have tried this umpteen ways), but something like:
> data {
>   int<lower=0>  N;// number of ppl
>   int<lower=0>  T;// number of timepoints
>   real x[T];      // X (time loadings)
>   real q[T];
>   real y[N,T];    // Y matrix of T obs of N ppl
>   int <lower=1> K;// number of classes
> }
> parameters {
>   simplex[K] pi;           // class weights
>   corr_matrix[3] Psi;      // prior correlation
>   vector<lower=0> [3] tau; // prior scale
>   vector[3] mu_eta[K];     // mean (int,slope,quad) for etas
>   vector[3] eta[N];        // etas (int,slope,quad) for each person
>   real<lower=0> sigmasq_y; // y error variance
> }

>   sigma_y<-sqrt(sigmasq_y);

> model {

>   real ps[K];
>   Sigma_eta<-quad_form_diag(Psi,tau);
>   mu_eta[K] ~ normal(0, 10);
>   tau~cauchy(0,2.5);
>   Psi~lkj_corr(2);
>   for (n in 1:N){
>     for (k in 1:K){
>       ps[k]<-log(pi[k])+ multi_normal_log(eta[n],mu_eta[k],Sigma_eta);
>     }
>     increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[n], eta[n,1]+eta[n,2]*x+eta[n,3]*q,sigma_y));
>     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
>   }
> }

> On Friday, March 27, 2015 at 12:22:30 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I can make several suggestions on model and implementation.
>
> First, don't use any of these priors:
>
>    mu_eta[K] ~ normal(0, 100);
>    sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001); //y residual error variance drawn from prior
>    Psi~ inv_wishart(3, Omega); //cov matrix among etas drawn from prior
>
> They're all problematic for both computational and statistical
> reasons.  The fat normal and inverse gamma are just too fat.
> the inverse Wishart usually doesn't make any sense.  These priors
> just get used by BUGS/JAGS becaus they're conjugate.  We discuss
> recommended alternatives in the manual chapter on regression.
>
> We recommend a Cholesky-parameterized, scaled correlation matrix with
> an LKJ prior for Psi, and at least weakly informative priors for the
> others.  There are references as to why in the manual, too.
>
> Computationally, you probably don't want to define all those variables
> as transformed parameters, because then they get written out at each
> iteration.
>
> I'm not sure what you're trying to do, but this doesn't make sense:
>
> >    for (n in 1:N)
> >      for (k in 1:K)
> >       tt[k]<-log(pi[k])+multi_normal_log(eta[n],mu_eta[k],Psi);
>

>

>
> >  for (n in 1:N){
> >    log_q_z[n]<-log(pi);
> >    for (t in 1:T)
> >      for(k in 1:K)

>
> // x        : T x 1
> // pi       : K x 1
> // eta:     : N x 3
> // q        : T x 1
> // sigma_y  : 1
>
> so there's nothing in that loop other that varies by k other than log_q_z.
> If that's really what you want (I don't really have time to figure it out),
> then you're far better of using vectorization on the normal_log over t
> outside of the loop over K --- as is, you're doing way too much extra
> work.
>
> So that'd be something like this:
>
> {
>   vector[K] log_pi;
>   log_pi <- log(pi);
>
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     real lp;
>     lp <- normal_log(y[n],
>                      eta[n,1] + eta[n,2] * x + eta[n,3] * q,
>                      sigma_y);
>     for (k in 1:K)
>       log_q_z[n,k] <- log_pi[k] + lp;
>   }
> }
>
> But I'm not convinced you're doing what you want to do here.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben!

Just to clarify: The wait function you show is part of the Stan model which you then call in R via the magic Rcpp trick which you formerly called "testify", right?

Awesome that this is already in Stan 2.6.3 which triggers, of course, immediately the question when this will be available as rstan or even better available on cran?

As I recall, the wrapped Stan functions always needed recompilation due to Rcpp - has there been a workaround for this, i.e. is a make-like behavior possible by now or should we direct this to the Rcpp maintainers? If Rcpp is the right address, what feature of Rcpp are you specifically using which one cannot cache like usual Stan model objects?

Best,
Sebastian

On Friday, March 27, 2015 at 11:13:10 PM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> I think the best way to do this is to user-define a Stan function that ends in _rng
>
> matrix foo_rng(matrix input) {
>   // do random-number generation
>   // return whatever
> }
>
> export that function to R (only rstan 2.6.3 is capable of doing this at the moment), and then call that function from R.
>
> E.g. I did this to calculate the WAIC from R
>
> # WAIC implied by normal log-likelihood
> vector WAIC(vector y, matrix X, /* N rows */
>             vector intercept, matrix beta,
>            /* parameters all have S draws */
>            vector sigma) {
>
>   vector[2] out; out <- rep_vector(0,2);
>   for(i in 1:rows(X)) {
>     vector[rows(beta)] ll;
>     vector[rows(beta)] mu; mu <- intercept +
>      beta * transpose(row(X,i));
>     for(j in 1:rows(beta)) ll[j] <-
>       normal_log(y[i], mu[j], sigma[j]);
>     out[1] <- out[1] + log(mean(exp(ll)));
>     out[2] <- out[2] + variance(ll);
>   }
>   out[1] <- -2 * (out[1] - out[2]);
>   return out; # out[1] is WAIC, out[2] is p_WAIC
> }
>
> Ben
>
> On Friday, March 27, 2015 at 5:51:11 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> > Hi—I thought of that but this is not so natural.  For example, suppose the parameter “a” in the model is a vector of length 2, and we run Stan and get 2000 simulations.  Then we’d have to declare “a” as a 2000 x 2 matrix.  But that is contrary to the spirit of probabilistic programming.
> >
> > > On Mar 27, 2015, at 5:24 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > It's technically possible -- you just have to convert the samples into data and then run a new model with those samples as data and the fixed_params sampler, which will execute  only the generated quantities block.

> > >

> > >> Hi, I’m stuck on something.  In some ways it’s no big deal cos I could do it in R, but I’d like to stay within Stan if possible.
> > >>
> > >> It’s a question about generated quantities, and it comes from the project with Sebastian and Amy on the incorporation of aggregate data into a Bayesian analysis.
> > >>
> > >> Currently I have a Stan program (attached in this message) that I wrote.  The program works as follows:
> > >>
> > >> - In the model block, I compute the log posterior given the data matrix y.
> > >>
> > >> - In the generated quantities block, I first simulate an external parameter delta (from a prior distribution input into the Stan model) and then I simulate a fake data matrix y_tilde.  For each posterior simulation draw (i.e., in each call to the generated quantities block), I simulate 100 fake data matrices and then compute their covariance matrix, then from there I compute an importance weight which is used in later calculations.
> > >>

As far as I know, it is not currently possible with Rcpp but it doesn't really have anything to do with Stan. If you just run Rcpp's example of sourceCpp, it does not work when reloaded in a new R session on the same computer

library(Rcpp)
sourceCpp(code='
  #include <Rcpp.h>

  // [[Rcpp::export]]
  int fibonacci(const int x) {
    if (x == 0) return(0);
    if (x == 1) return(1);
    return (fibonacci(x - 1)) + fibonacci(x - 2);
  }'
)
fibonacci(5) # 5
saveRDS(fibonacci, file = "fibonacci.rda")
q()

and then restart R

library(Rcpp)
fibonacci <- readRDS("fibonacci.rda")
fibonacci(5) # error

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

>From what I have seen an example models R package is planned - is that right?

I understood that this package pretty much includes all those very standard examples which are around, i.e. ARM and WinBUGS manual examples. Would it be possible to include the "original" BUGS files along with the Stan model codes? Reasons to do this:

- People know the BUGS stuff and can then easily compare what changes when going from BUGS to Stan.
- Also: WinBUGS is the golden reference when it comes to Bayesian statistics (at least this is its reputation in many fields). Hence, having the BUGS code nearby makes it easy for everyone to quickly cross-check that BUGS gives the exact same answer (whenever the model is sound, which those inverse-gamma priors may defeat).

Also: When is the example-models planned to see the light of this world?

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject_clean: postdoc opportunity in epidemiology at University of Michigan
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Stan users!  Jon Zelner points us to a postdoc opening on social/epi modeling at University of Michigan.  If you are interested, contact Dr. Eisenberg (see below) directly.
Andrew

—

Jon Zelner writes:

Just wanted to forward this along in case there was anyone you knew of who might be a good fit for this postdoc with my PhD advisor, Joe Eisenberg, at U-M Public Health. I think they particularly need someone with good quantitative/modeling skills, even if they don't have a public health background but are interested in getting into it. I can vouch for Joe being a great mentor/advisor who really looks out for his students and postdocs.

—

Postdoctoral position in Modeling Social and Environmental Influences on Waterborne Pathogen and Helminth Transmission available on a NSF-funded project (epidemiology/infectious diseases/transmission dynamics/enteric and helminth pathogens/environmental health/social networks/agent-based modeling)

Department of Epidemiology, School of Public Health, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

The Department of Epidemiology at the University of Michigan seeks to hire one postdoctoral fellow with interest and skills in analytical methods for estimating how social and physical environments interact to influence the transmission of waterborne pathogens. Support for the position is now available for up to two years through a NSF Water Sustainability and Climate grant entitled “Analytical methods for estimating the joint climatological-social drivers of water quality and supply in contrasting tropical zones: Ecuador and China.”  The grant includes faculty in Epidemiology (Joe Eisenberg, Michigan), Anthropology (Jim Trostle, Trinity College), and Environmental Health (Justin Remais, Emory).

The successful applicant will be a productive scholar who combines an interest in modeling complex human/environment interactions with skills and knowledge related to how vulnerability and adaptive capacity impact communities responding to climate change. The ideal candidate has quantitative background and a PhD in disease ecology, epidemiology, anthropology, geography, sociology, or other integrative field; previous experience in modeling epidemiological or ecological systems; and previous high-quality, first-authored publications. The fellow will help to develop agent-based, system dynamic, or network models as appropriate, and to develop region-specific scenarios based on specific processes that mediate how water quality and waterborne disease transmission respond to climate variability, management decisions, and coping capacity at the village level. Knowledge of Spanish or Chinese is a plus but not required.

The University of Michigan offers a vibrant mathematical modeling and complex systems community. Modeling expertise extends across departments including Epidemiology, Health Management and Policy, Complex Systems, Population Center, Institute for Social Research, and Ecology and Evolutionary Biology. The School of Public Health is renowned for its cutting edge research on the applications of mathematical modeling in epidemiology and public health.

Applicants must have completed all requirements for a doctoral degree in a relevant field from an accredited program before they begin the fellowship. Applicants must have a record of accomplishment in modeling and systems science demonstrated in their publications and research background.  Initial appointments will be for one year, with possibility of renewal.  The salary will be in the range of $45,000 per year (depending on experience), plus fringe benefits.  Compensation (salary and benefits) will be offered according to University of Michigan and NSF guidelines.

To apply please submit CV, names of references, and inquiries to Dr. Joseph Eisenberg, Professor of Epidemiology, at jn...@umich.edu.  Starting date is negotiable. Applicants should send a cover letter, a detailed CV, a brief statement of research interests, and the names of three references to Dr. Joseph Eisenberg at jn...@umich.edu. The position will remain open until filled.

Joseph Eisenberg

Department of Epidemiology

School of Public Health

University of Michigan

1415 Washington Heights

Ann Arbor, MI  48109

messages.body_plain:
Thanks. Here is the JAGS code.

I'm still struggling with how to easily translate it to stan. Thanks again.

model{
  for(i in 1:n){  # n is respondent
    for (j in 1:p){ #Loop over item, p is item
      y[i,j]~dcat(prob[i,j,1:K[j]])
    }
    theta[i]~dnorm(0, 1)
    for (j in 1:p){ #Loop over item, p is item
      for (k in 1:(K[j]-1)){ #Loop over K-1 response categories
        logit(P[i,j,k])<-alpha[j]*theta[i] -kappa[j,k]
      }
      P[i,j,K[j]]<-1

    }
    for (j in 1:p){

      prob[i,j,1]<-P[i,j,1]
      for (k in 2:K[j])
        prob[i,j,k]<-P[i,j,k]-P[i,j,k-1]
      }
    }
  }
  #Specify priors/hyperpriors for alpha

  for (j in 1:p){

    alpha[j]~dnorm(mu,prec)
  }

  mu~dnorm(1,0.01)I(0,) #alpha should be positive -- this is the discrimination parameter.
  prec~dgamma(1,.1)

  for (j in 1:p){

    kappa0[j,1]~dunif(-3,3)
    for (k in 2:K[j]-1){
      kappa0[j,k]~dunif(kappa0[j,k-1],3)
    }
    kappa[j,1:K[j]-1]<-sort(kappa0[j,1:K[j]-1])

  }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] example model package coming?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] example model package coming?
messages.body_plain:
I think that "a direct translation from the BUGS models to Stan" may be useful, but the models should have BIG WARNING LABEL that the models and priors may be really bad.
If people google models, they should find models and priors based on the latest best practices. There should be a page explaining the generic changes made to the models.
I'm willing to help to update BUGS models, but maybe there should first be the page providing the guidelines for updating the BUGS models, and then any volunteer could use those guidelines to update some model and submit it for further checking by the Stan authorities.

Aki
